issues.body:
Automated tracking issue for failures of the `skyrl-nightly` scheduled run.

Each failure adds a comment below with the run link and a log excerpt, and asks
a weaver session to triage. A repository-local fix PR should close this issue
with a Fixes link. If no fix PR is warranted, close the issue once the lane
is green again. The next failure opens a fresh issue.

🤖 **Research:** In [run 45878870665](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/45878870665/job/140112802997), the Grug job failed before submission. `google-github-actions/setup-gcloud@v3` authenticated, then `gcloud --quiet config set project hai-gcp-models` failed while refreshing its WIF token: `RemoteDisconnected('Remote end closed connection without response')`. issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Mochi .129 archives can report `generated_tokens=0` when a turn deadline cancels a long active decode before a complete non-streaming ModelTurn reaches the recorder. This does not establish that the inference engine generated no tokens. The original blanket engine-queue-starvation diagnosis was unsupported.

The balanced 500-rollout sample contains 58 such timeout rows (11.6%). In the learner's separate consumed-batch cohort, 363/12,800 rows were verifier-unavailable (2.84%); they were token-loss masked and excluded from RLOO baselines, not trained as reward-zero failures.

Retained timing events match 29 of the 58 sampled session IDs and cover 32 request IDs with 115–19,735 generated tokens. Internal queue wait was at most 18.529 s and first-token delay at most 19.773 s. Last observed decode spans reach 1,743.155 s (median 1,291.646 s), mostly from progress events rather than completed requests. These aggregates include three sessions outside a coarse timing check. Session reuse, Ray log suppression and unobserved pre-engine waits prevent a strict causal fraction for all 58 rows. No retained event demonstrates an engine admission wait approaching 1,800 s; the overall queue-starvation share remains unknown.

The same run's step-24 Micro210 evaluation originally scored 365/434 trials. The existing BixBench regrade brings that to 375/434; the user authorized recovery of only the remaining 58 no-response slots and one verifier timeout, keeping all 375 graded outcomes unchanged.

Private sample: `open-athena/mochi-rl-129-rollout-sample`, `rollouts.parquet`, e.g. `transcripts/0125.md`. Run record: marin-community/marin-logbooks#88. Evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/mochi-zero-token-timeouts/2026.11.26.1/deadline-correction-evidence.json`.

Expected: retain the exact partial generation when an active decode reaches its deadline and run the real verifier under #10197. A genuinely never-scheduled request must use a distinct bounded admission allowance. Output length and slow decode under load need separate attribution.

Done when:

- Active deadline expiry returns exact sampled tokens, behavior logprobs, routes and policy-step stamps for verification, without a synthetic EOS or a fabricated completed response. Apply the contract to canonical evaluation as well as future authored Mochi RL recipes.
- Preserve the user's slot-ownership-clock requirement: execution budgets start/resume at actual engine scheduling, with a saturated-slot regression. This is a guard against real admission wait, not an established explanation of the sampled cohort.
- Report queue wait separately from generation time, and attribute slow decode with per-request/per-engine evidence rather than inferring it from a zero-token archive.
- Confirm unavailable rows are excluded from token loss and RLOO baselines. This masking check is complete.

Partial-retention implementation 0602a5bbdc is landed and enabled by future Mochi RL recipes; admission-clock implementation e6aeaa1813/1802d95806 is landed through 77f3e5f57a. Already submitted jobs remain pinned. Shared task-client partial return is now landed in 36098e90e2, covering future canonical evaluation without a protocol override. The already submitted exact-59 recovery remains on 77f3. GPU runtime certification and slow-decode attribution remain open.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

On [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120), the total-turn timer starts when the first model request is sent, and the model-turn timer also covers engine queue time. vLLM already records QUEUED and SCHEDULED events with per-request queue wait, but that signal stays in engine logs; the model client returns only after generation. The outer attempt timer starts before harness execution, while the zero-token unavailable row appears to have both loss and baseline eligibility disabled; the latter still needs an end-to-end assertion.

**Relevant code**
- [`recorder.py#L222-L236`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f431fe52c3f14b03f616d6f38330eb2403447e3/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py#L222-L236) — total-turn deadline starts on send
- [`recorder.py#L358-L369`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f431fe52c3f14b03f616d6f38330eb2403447e3/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py#L358-L369) — model-turn deadline includes queue time
- [`engine.py#L162-L168`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f431fe52c3f14b03f616d6f38330eb2403447e3/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/engine.py#L162-L168) — attempt deadline starts before harness
- [`request_timing.py#L35-L85`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f431fe52c3f14b03f616d6f38330eb2403447e3/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/request_timing.py#L35-L85) — scheduler events and queue-wait evidence
- [`task_projections.py#L199-L223`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6f431fe52c3f14b03f616d6f38330eb2403447e3/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L199-L223) — unavailable-row training disposition

# Proposed Fix

This spans the rollout engine, SkyRL inference transport, Harbor trial limits, and trainer evidence, so it belongs on #11120 or a coordinated follow-up after that branch lands. #11120 is open and currently conflicts with `main`; a separate implementation PR would duplicate its branch-only rollout engine.

1. Carry a request-ID-correlated SCHEDULED notification from the vLLM engine to the pending model call. Start total-turn and model-turn budgets on first engine scheduling, including long prefill and decode. Bound pre-scheduling wait with a separate queue-admission deadline, and preserve a separate setup watchdog. Align the outer attempt and Harbor trial clocks with that lifecycle so neither can cancel a queued first request.
2. Reuse the existing per-request QUEUED/SCHEDULED/first-token timing to emit queue wait and generation durations as separate rollout metrics. Propagate them into SkyRL's train/eval telemetry; include cancelled and never-scheduled requests in queue diagnostics.
3. Add a saturated-engine regression: hold all slots beyond the turn timeout, queue a short request, confirm it remains pending, then release a slot and confirm its deadline begins. Cover a request that never gets scheduled under the queue deadline. Add a trainer test for a zero-token unavailable row that checks zero loss mask, baseline exclusion, and zero advantage with the configured estimator; document the observed disposition.

Validate with the affected CPU tests and a bounded mixed-source replay, comparing its zero-token timeout count and score coverage against the issue's 58/500 train and 69/434 Micro210 baselines.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Correction from the follow-up investigation. The diagnosis in the issue body (deadline before engine-slot ownership, queue starvation) is contradicted by the engine data.

- **Masked, not trained as zero:** all 58 sampled zero-token rows were masked and excluded from the RLOO baseline. In `.129`'s 25 consumed batches, 363 of 12,800 trajectories were verifier-unavailable (2.84%), and 395 were masked overall.
- **The engines did generate:** for the 29 affected sessions with engine timing, they generated 115 to 19,735 tokens. Queue wait was at most 18.5 s and time to first token at most 19.8 s. Across all 80 engine snapshots, the most requests running at once were 19 (`.129`) and 18 (`.131`), against a limit of 64. "Turn deadline expired before the first response" means no *completed* non-streaming response. The outer 1800 s deadline discarded unfinished generations.
- **Rates in the uniform 10% retained archives:** `.129` 212/1,786 = 11.87%; `.131` 194/2,083 = 9.31%. All of them are masked.
- **Fix, future runs only:** `0602a5bbdc` on `benfeuer/long-loop-prototype`. At 1770 s, inside the unchanged 1800 s turn deadline, active requests are returned through vLLM's partial-output abort. Real tokens, logprobs and routes are preserved, the actual verifier runs, and no further turn is allowed. Requests with no tokens stay unavailable. `.131` is unchanged.
- **Evidence:** the investigation report in #12267 (comment 7182161172), Echo incident wiki/1087, and `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/mochi-zero-token-timeouts/2026.11.26.1/investigation-record.json`.

The slot-ownership clock requirement remains as a guard. The measured queue share is small (seconds), but a trial's clock should still start only when it owns an engine slot.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 Landed the engine-admission clock fix via loop-push at [77f3e5f57a](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/77f3e5f57ad298b72b0647bbce309e8af9ac85f1) (implementation e6aeaa1813; installed-agent HTTP propagation 1802d95806).

The recorder, attempt and Harbor phase execution budgets now receive the actual vLLM SCHEDULED/first-token notification through the cancellable request stream. Waiting before admission uses a separate cumulative 2,280-second allowance; it no longer consumes execution time. Setup and detached-agent watchdogs remain bounded. Never-scheduled requests become admission timeouts, not pre-token total_turn_timeout. Queue wait and generation time are separate rollout metrics.

Masking answer: verifier-unavailable rows were not trained as reward-zero failures. [Task projections](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/77f3e5f57ad298b72b0647bbce309e8af9ac85f1/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L393) set token loss mask 0 and exclude them from the RLOO baseline; [normalized verifier scores](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/77f3e5f57ad298b72b0647bbce309e8af9ac85f1/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/trajectory_processing.py#L133) remain unavailable. The real projection + RLOO regression produces loss masks [1,1,0] and advantages [1,-1,0] for win/loss/unavailable. In .129's 25 consumed batches, 363/12,800 rows were verifier-unavailable; this denominator differs from the balanced 500-rollout sample, whose 58 zero-response timeouts were all masked.

The saturated-slot regression fails on clean0602 and passes after the fix. Landing checks passed: 260 rolloutengine, 54 SkyRL, 5 subset-identity and 33 Harbor queue/deadline tests, plus lint/types. The affected runner's 13 Harbor failures independently reproduce on clean0602; this is not a broad-suite pass. No GPU correctness claim yet.

Latest user clarification protects 375 already graded outcomes, including the ten prior BixBench regrades, and authorizes only 59 recoveries: 58 no-response trials and one verifier timeout. The earlier 69-slot job was cancelled after this clarification; its GPU child is terminal KILLED on all four tasks, and none of its results will be adopted. The corrected canonical recovery is `/benfeuer/long-loop-mochi-v5-exp3-rl-micro210-infra-recovery59-2026.11.26.3-coordinator-3a1256aa`, on the same landed clock fix. Its manifest pins the 365 original native rows plus ten prior BixBench graded rows, with no BixBench identity selected for generation. Seeds, task bytes, model and frozen protocol remain unchanged. Final sealing requires the exact 375+59 merge, trace audit and at least 391 valid results out of the fixed 434-row cohort. No final score yet; .131 remains unchanged.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **Diagnostic correction:** the original blanket queue-starvation explanation is unsupported. An archived `generated_tokens=0` means no complete non-streaming `ModelTurn` reached the recorder; it does not mean vLLM generated no tokens. Cancelling a long active decode at the turn deadline can discard its exact partial response. The [recorder contract](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/77f3e5f57ad298b72b0647bbce309e8af9ac85f1/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py#L173) makes this distinction explicit.

- **Masking:** .129's 25 consumed batches contain **363/12,800 verifier-unavailable rows (2.84%)**. They were masked from token loss and excluded from the RLOO baseline, **not trained as reward 0**. The balanced 500-rollout sample's 58 timeout rows (11.6%) use a different denominator.
- **Engine join:** 29 of the 58 sampled session IDs have 44 retained timing events covering 32 request IDs, with **115–19,735 generated tokens**. Internal queue wait was at most **18.529 s**; first-token delay was at most **19.773 s**.
- **Decode time:** last observed first-token-to-last-token spans were **9.073–1,743.155 s**, median **1,291.646 s**. Thirty of the 32 final observations are progress events, so these are mostly **right-censored lower bounds**, not completed decode durations. The two retained ended events span 9.073 s and 1,602.944 s. Examples that pass the coarse timing check: session `19830_3` had 14,615 tokens after 1,743.155 s, and `11198_5` had 17,397 after 1,741.821 s.
- **Join limits:** those aggregates include all 29 session-ID matches; only 26 pass a coarse previous-optimizer-through-step+4 timing check. Session reuse and Ray log suppression prevent a strict per-invocation join. In particular, the short 9.073 s ended request belongs to a session outside that check.
- **Real queue-wait share:** no retained event shows a 1,800 s engine admission wait. This is **not a measured 0% for all 58 failures**: 29 sampled session IDs have no joined evidence, and internal vLLM timing excludes pre-engine waits. The total causal share is **unknown**. The user's slot-ownership-clock guard remains a separate Done-when requirement; the saturated-slot regression demonstrates the code gap, not that it caused this cohort.

[Partial-retention fix 0602a5bbdc](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0602a5bbdc91d2f548d96b9f9ecb7404395b9261) uses vLLM's abort/output path to return exact sampled tokens, logprobs, routes and policy stamps, then invokes the real verifier under #10197; it synthesizes no EOS. Its 1,770 s cutoff, leaving 30 s inside the 1,800 s turn budget, is enabled in future authored Mochi RL recipes. [77f3e5f57a](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/77f3e5f57ad298b72b0647bbce309e8af9ac85f1) separately preserves execution budgets during admission. Neither changes an already submitted .129/.131 process.

**Shared adoption is now fixed for future jobs** by [36098e90e2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/36098e90e2ea69f2beebfd3d76ba0c218cbb828e). The clock-aware task client requests the native partial abort before its nearest remaining trial/turn/agent deadline, including time spent in earlier turns, then awaits the original response collector. It needs no recipe-specific cutoff or frozen-protocol override. Caller cancellation remains cancellation; requests that generated no tokens remain unavailable. Both raw and chat paths retain exact token metadata. Clean-base regressions fail before the fix and pass afterward; CPU checks passed (58 related SkyRL and 260 rolloutengine tests). Broader checks have 12 independently reproduced baseline Harbor failures, not a broad-suite pass. No GPU certification is claimed.

The active exact-59 recovery remains pinned to 77f3 and has no 1,770 s engine cutoff; **the new shared partial-return fix is not active in that submitted job**. It continues unchanged, protecting all 375 prior grades.

There are also 12 retained same-request decode intervals; all show positive token progress, with interval-average rates **8.726–12.724 tokens/s**, median **10.271**. Long outputs at these rates explain how a short prompt can consume most of a 1,800 s turn budget. These sparse intervals do not exclude shorter stalls or identify whether kernel/expert-collective contention, weight synchronization or another load effect limits the rate. **Slow-decode attribution remains open.** [Interval evidence](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fmochi-zero-token-timeouts%2F2026.11.26.1%2Fdecode-intervals-evidence.json): `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/mochi-zero-token-timeouts/2026.11.26.1/decode-intervals-evidence.json`.

The title already matches “Turn-deadline expiry discards partial generations as zero-token rollouts”; the issue body has been corrected. [Retained evidence](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fbenfeuer%2Fmochi-zero-token-timeouts%2F2026.11.26.1%2Fdeadline-correction-evidence.json): `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/users/benfeuer/mochi-zero-token-timeouts/2026.11.26.1/deadline-correction-evidence.json`.

The [partial-return change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0602a5bbdc91d2f548d96b9f9ecb7404395b9261) addresses active decodes, while the [admission-clock change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e6aeaa1813) and [shared task-client change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/36098e90e2) preserve the clock and return partial output for canonical evaluation. These commits are on draft #11120 and are absent from `main`.

I’ll port the shared runtime and transport contract onto `main`, including installed-agent callbacks from [1802d95806](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/1802d95806), with regressions for partial token metadata, saturated admission and never-scheduled requests. This targets the reported 78/434 discarded Micro210 rows in future evaluations. The archived zero-token count alone does not establish engine starvation, and this CPU code port does not certify GPU runtime behavior.

🤖 Opened standalone PR [#12392](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12392) against `main`. It ports partial-generation retention and scheduling-based admission clocks from draft #11120 into the current shared task client. Future canonical Micro210 evaluations can grade exact sampled tokens, logprobs, routes, and policy-step stamps when an active decode reaches its deadline. A separate per-attempt allowance bounds admission wait; transports without scheduling notices retain the prior turn deadline. The recorder attributes retained partials to the model-turn, total-turn, or attempt budget. Queue wait and generation time are reported separately, with request and engine IDs in timing evidence.

Local lint and type checks passed. Focused tests passed: 277 RolloutEngine, 11 Shellbox, and 55 SkyRL transport/task tests. The broad root test runner stopped before collection because its environment lacks `pytest-xdist`; package-level suites used their configured environments. GPU runtime certification and slow-decode attribution remain open under this issue. All required CI checks are green after retrying the Levanter serialization shard, which failed twice in untouched tests. The PR is ready for review.

issues.title: [rl] Turn-deadline expiry discards partial generations as zero-token rollouts

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
At 128 outstanding requests on one H100x8 node, immediate refill completed the same two-wave Snowball input workload **28.4–30.6% sooner** than burst/drain across three warmed pairs. The short four-node confirmation reduced elapsed time from **237.75 to 164.12 seconds (31.0%)** at 512 outstanding requests. These are serving measurements; they do not establish an RL-step speedup.

Follow-up to #8765. Linked implementation drafts: [MSRL telemetry and benchmark](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/515); [Marin diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8930).

## Matched comparison

Each one-node arm processes 256 requests from the same frozen waves `[1,2]`, with 128 outstanding at most. Burst waits for each 128-request wave to finish; refill replaces each completion immediately. Order was AB, BA, AB after warmup. Each arm starts with an empty prefix cache, retains reuse within the arm, and uses the same checkpoint, sampling, token limits, production client, and session hash routing.

| Pair | Burst seconds | Refill seconds | Time saved | Burst / refill whole-arm tokens/s | Output-token change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 178.25 | 127.23 | 28.62% | 4,289 / 6,166 | +2.62% |
| B | 179.72 | 124.77 | 30.58% | 4,484 / 6,329 | −2.02% |
| C | 181.10 | 129.71 | 28.38% | 4,405 / 6,142 | −0.13% |

Individual burst waves took about 88–92 seconds. Refill's whole-arm token throughput increased 39.4–43.8%, while native token-weighted ITL rose from 11.25–11.46 ms to 12.41–12.60 ms. Request p99 rose from about 90–92 seconds to 101–104 seconds. Aggregate utilization improved while each active sequence ran somewhat slower.

The four-node pair processed 1,024 requests per arm. Burst produced 3,243,913 tokens at 13,644 tokens/s; refill produced 3,182,271 at 19,389 tokens/s, a 42.1% rate increase with 1.9% fewer output tokens. Its burst waves took 121.67 and 116.08 seconds. Refill had a 30-second qualifying steady interval at 31,635 tokens/s; this is distinct from its whole-arm rate. One four-node pair confirms direction, without establishing scaling efficiency.

Natural stopping remains enabled. The generator seed is fixed, but per-request random streams and batching are not forced identical. Output totals and length-finish fractions vary; the paired output differences above bound an observed workload difference, not all uncertainty. Three pairs and one topology confirmation do not support a formal confidence interval.

## Sustained-load tradeoff

Steady rates use complete per-engine collection intervals from ten seconds after treatment start through the last request submission. The finite sweep pools contain 256, 512, 768, and 1,536 requests respectively, drawn from the same six-wave corpus; they are not identical cohorts. Latency and ITL columns summarize the whole arm, including its drain.

| Outstanding, one node | Steady seconds | Generated tokens/s | Completions/s | Request p50 / p99, s | Native mean ITL, ms | Peak observed KV |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 115 | 5,375 | 1.43 | 24.6 / 97.5 | 11.61 | 5.3% |
| 128 | 115 | 9,490 | 2.94 | 24.2 / 110.6 | 13.06 | 9.7% |
| 256 | 95 | 16,827 | 4.30 | 31.7 / 123.9 | 14.70 | 17.2% |
| 512 | 125 | 27,417 | 6.76 | 36.1 / 151.9 | 17.81 | 32.9% |

No sampled waiting requests or vLLM preemptions occurred. Throughput had not plateaued at 512, but latency, ITL, and KV use had increased. Length-finish fractions were 18.8%, 17.8%, 18.8%, and 19.3%; the output cap was 8,192 tokens. First-token p90 increased from 99 ms at 64 to 260 ms at 512. Five-second samples can miss short peaks.

For the next sustained-serving experiment, **256 outstanding per node is a useful starting point if the observed roughly 124-second request p99 is acceptable**: it gave 77% more steady token throughput than 128, with about 12% higher p99 and no observed queueing. Keep 128 for the production-sized control or a tighter latency budget. Use 512 only with room for the observed roughly 152-second p99. These are measured tradeoffs on this corpus, not established service limits or a proposal to change RL scheduling.

## Historical fidelity and rebounds

The historical `/power/grug-megatron-snowball-r5-final-2` phases took 134.693 and 134.048 seconds for 512 requests across four H100x8 rollout nodes. This replay preserves its stock wheel, model source identity, DP8/EP8/TP1, token caps, natural stopping, grouping and session routing, but **does not reproduce those exact trajectories or the exact 134-second wall**. The new four-node bursts are about 10–13% shorter. The frozen SFT export and sampled curriculum are explicit; historical config requested `resume_mode=latest`, and the exact restored weight state was not recovered here. There is no concurrent training. The within-replay paired result is the causal comparison; extrapolating its magnitude to the historical run remains open.

The six clean one-node burst waves had **no positive adjacent increase in complete five-second raw generation-rate intervals**. Large rises aligned with the next wave submission. Token-weighted ITL fell from roughly 12.3 toward 10 ms during draining, while aggregate generation fell as fewer requests remained.

For the first burst pair, all 320 landed generation-counter records matched raw cumulative samples from all eight engines. Maximum observed publication lag was 0.413 seconds. The production token-rate SQL's 13 fixed 15-second bins matched reconstruction to under `1e-9` tokens/s. Twelve full bins had 24 samples each; the final partial bin had only eight samples but retained the 15-second denominator, an edge-window artifact. There were no counter resets or missing producers. A historical within-wave rebound is not reproduced or explained by this result; retain exact historical requests/weight state and repeat the raw-counter audit if it recurs.

## Profiles and hypotheses

Stock native PyTorch profiles captured early decode on 8/8 EP ranks, steady refill on all 32 participating ranks across four nodes, and a fresh-process drained tail on 8/8 ranks. Nearby raw snapshots show 98–116 running requests around early capture, 512 during steady refill, and 27–28 during the tail. AllGather and ReduceScatter kernels are present on the participating ranks.

NCCL accounted for 14.9–20.2% of summed GPU kernel duration across early ranks, 18.1–22.7% across tail ranks, and 29.6–37.7% across the four-node steady captures. These fractions are not wall critical-path time, link bandwidth, or an isolated communication penalty; the captures differ in load and topology. They support communication attribution, not a communication-bottleneck claim.

Two-second capture requests caused 19–28-second profile/export wall windows. Restarting the profiler in the original engine process hit a CUDA launch failure; the incomplete `profile-burst` arm has 42 request errors, retained in the artifact. Fresh-process steady and tail captures succeeded. Every profiled arm is excluded from clean performance results.

| Hypothesis | Status and evidence | Remaining discriminator |
|---|---|---|
| Burst draining leaves serving capacity unused | Confirmed in this replay: repeated refill reduced whole-workload time at the same outstanding limit | Exact historical trajectories and restored weights before transferring the effect size |
| Fewer active requests necessarily make each output token slower | Rejected for these clean draining intervals: native ITL decreased as aggregate throughput fell | Hold context and occupancy independently for a kernel-level causal claim |
| Queueing, KV exhaustion, or vLLM preemption explains these clean tails | Rejected within observed intervals: zero waiting/preemptions, low KV in matched arms | Finer samples if a short transient is suspected |
| A within-wave throughput rebound is present | Not reproduced in six clean waves; observed large rises start the next wave | Capture the exact historical workload and audit raw producers when it recurs |
| NCCL is the limiting cause | Open: all-rank traces identify collective work, without isolating its critical-path cost | Matched occupancy/context profiles or a controlled communication experiment |
| 512 outstanding reaches the throughput ceiling | Open: throughput still increased, with higher latency/KV | Extend a repeated sweep only if the latency budget permits |

## Telemetry and dashboard validation

Native ITL previously missed the histogram allowlist. The MSRL draft forwards all 20 buckets plus count and sum at the existing five-second cadence whenever telemetry is enabled. Opt-in benchmark artifacts retain unaggregated per-engine snapshots, poll times, counter baselines, treatment boundaries, compact request/group/engine IDs, submission/first-token/completion times, lengths and outcomes. First-token time is the wrapper's first nonempty output. Generated text and per-token dumps are omitted; request IDs never become Finelog labels.

All complete clean arms reconciled generated-token and finished-request counter deltas exactly with receipts, with no missing timings, unknown engines, histogram failures, resets, or collection errors. One-node raw capture has 570 snapshots and 33,967,312 bytes; four-node capture has 168 snapshots and 38,324,159 bytes. The only request errors belong to the excluded failed profile attempt.

Live 30-second Finelog windows contained 1,056 native ITL records for eight engines and 4,224 for 32, exactly six polls per engine. All available dropped-record counters remained zero. ITL adds 35.2 records/s per node; total observed native telemetry was 338 records/s on one node and 1,350.8 on four. Mean poll collection plus publication cost was 96.4 ms on one node and 325.4 ms on four, against a five-second cadence (1.93% and 6.51% of driver wall time). These component costs exclude raw JSON encoding/writing and are not an on/off estimate of serving-throughput overhead. Actual poll spacing stayed approximately 5.001 seconds.

The Marin draft adds native output-length distributions in numeric bucket order, explicit cap annotation, length-finish fraction, and per-engine ITL beside existing per-engine throughput. All 17 provisioned data panels returned populated rows through the modified local bridge using real Finelog data. The length view reconciled 128 requests and 30 length finishes (23.4375%); all eight per-engine ITL values were present. The new dashboard has not been deployed.

At the initial Marin draft head `4ace1ba5eb91`, the full baseline and changed overview queries both exceeded Finelog's ten-second deadline on the same dense 185-second window. The shorter live panel smoke and standalone token-rate SQL succeeded. The query-cost follow-up below records the subsequent repair and matched wider-window validation.

Fixed-window links to the existing dashboard (new panels require deploying the draft): [validated short window](https://grafana.oa.dev/d/marin-inference/marin-inference?from=1788572557000&to=1788572670000&var-identity_kind=run_id&var-identity=snowball-throughput-20260905-one-node&var-output_cap=8192), [one-node burst/refill](https://grafana.oa.dev/d/marin-inference/marin-inference?from=1788572752210&to=1788573673244&var-identity_kind=run_id&var-identity=snowball-throughput-20260905-one-node&var-output_cap=8192), [four-node native-telemetry window](https://grafana.oa.dev/d/marin-inference/marin-inference?from=1788576120000&to=1788576150000&var-identity_kind=run_id&var-identity=snowball-throughput-20260905-four-node&var-output_cap=8192). These links target production; the candidate query repair below has only been validated locally.

## Inference dashboard query cost (2026-09-05)

The revised bridge in #8930 (`88b2fd7efd9d5cf7080033429acaea3b2d6e94e7`) returns all seven matched windows below. Six timed out with the original draft (`4ace1ba5eb91cd184dec17c704ec7aa5962a9ac3`). Live Finelog `EXPLAIN` shows 100 scan operators in the original overview and two in the candidate. The candidate fetches compact per-series samples once, computes the existing diagnostics locally, and shares the result across panels and both pages.

Each arm used the same identity, exact window, 15-second bucket request, serve/run selector, and parallel panel requests. The overview opened first, diagnostics reused its result, and both pages repeated warm. Finelog time is client wall time summed over the selector and overview calls; page time ends when the first page’s API requests finish. These are individual replay samples, not browser-paint measurements or a fleet load test.

| Window | Millisecond bounds [from, to) | Before Finelog / page seconds | After Finelog / page seconds |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| One node, validated short | `1788572557000, 1788572670000` | 13.983 / 14.016 (data) | 1.042 / 2.065 (data) |
| One node, failing 185 s | `1788572750000, 1788572935000` | 11.172 / 11.197 (timeout) | 1.336 / 2.488 (data) |
| Four nodes, failing 30 s | `1788576120000, 1788576150000` | 10.820 / 10.840 (timeout) | 9.597 / 10.232 (data) |
| One node, full comparison | `1788572752210, 1788573673244` | 15.745 / 15.774 (timeout) | 2.055 / 4.335 (data) |
| Four nodes, full comparison | `1788576085551, 1788576487512` | 11.837 / 11.854 (timeout) | 1.671 / 5.664 (data) |
| One node, chosen 5 min | `1788573373244, 1788573673244` | 11.439 / 11.458 (timeout) | 0.947 / 1.843 (data) |
| Four nodes, chosen 5 min | `1788575850000, 1788576150000` | 11.391 / 11.411 (timeout) | 1.100 / 3.022 (data) |

Each cold sequence made two Finelog calls: one selector and one shared data query. Opening the second dashboard and repeating both pages warm made zero additional calls. All candidate panels returned HTTP 200. The slow four-node sample remains in the table: its selector took 3.948 seconds and its compact query took 5.649 seconds; the complete page took 10.232 seconds. The server’s ten-second query deadline is unchanged. A separate run of the checked-in replay completed that window in 2.595 seconds. This does not establish a whole-page latency guarantee. A matched run with diagnostics opening first timed out at 10.813 seconds before the change and returned all candidate panels in 2.311 seconds; overview and both warm pages then made zero additional Finelog calls.

A real 120-second refresh advanced the one-node five-minute window to `[1788573493244, 1788573793244)`. The original query timed out again after 14.262 seconds. The candidate returned the new window in 1.994 seconds with two Finelog calls; diagnostics then reused it with zero calls. The new window’s 444 output rows matched the original calculation on the same input samples. Defaults change from three hours / one minute to five minutes / two minutes.

The live short-window baseline and candidate match across all panel rows, including 128 output lengths, 30 length finishes (23.4375%), and eight per-engine ITL values. The maximum numeric difference is 9.1e-13. For the six denser windows, the unchanged original SQL was evaluated locally on the identical Finelog inputs, without the candidate’s input trimming: all 3,699 ordered rows and fields match, with maximum numeric difference 1.1e-11. The focused tests also cover producer separation, counter resets, coherent histograms, missing ITL in MSRL and standalone vLLM, changed windows, and missing versus zero.

The fetch rejects more than one million samples or 50,000 series instead of returning partial diagnostics. DuckDB calculations run one at a time with one thread, a 512 MB managed-memory limit, and disk spilling disabled. The full four-node local calculation took 4.493 seconds; peak process RSS was 596 MiB (609,924 KiB). This moves bounded work to the Grafana bridge. Dense historical windows can still require narrowing. The maximum selectable range remains seven days, and missing historical ITL remains unavailable. [MarinSkyRL PR #515](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/515) is needed to populate ITL on other MSRL exporters, not to merge this query change.

Both candidate dashboards were provisioned and rendered locally with Grafana 13.1.1 and Infinity 3.10.1, using the candidate bridge over captured real Arrow inputs. The output-length buckets remained numerically ordered, the 8,192-token cap annotation rendered, and the length-finish and engine panels were present. The production-style container build reached dependency installation and dashboard stitching but failed during image export when local disk filled. The local render used the matching upstream Grafana image after removing only this task’s build cache. No production deployment or new inference run was performed.

Reproduce from the repository root with the replay in this PR:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=infra/grafana/src uv run python infra/grafana/benchmarks/inference_query_cost.py \
  --identity snowball-throughput-20260905-four-node \
  --from-ms 1788576120000 --to-ms 1788576150000 \
  --output /tmp/inference-query-after
```

For the baseline, extract `infra/grafana/src` and `infra/grafana/dashboards` from `4ace1ba5eb91cd184dec17c704ec7aa5962a9ac3` with `git archive`. Set `PYTHONPATH` to the extracted `src/`, pass its parent as `--grafana-dir`, and use a different output directory. Use the bounds above for the other windows, `--first-page diagnostics` to reverse page order, and `--refresh-after 120` for an actual refresh. The replay writes every SQL request, Arrow input, response, query count/time, and page latency. It uses existing read-only Finelog data; repeat only the needed windows.

The final `cd infra/grafana && uv run pytest` suite passed 258 tests. Owning lint passed. The repository’s affected-test selector selected zero packages for these Grafana files, so the explicit bridge suite is the test evidence.

Independent Claude and Codex goal reviews found no material implementation defect. Their error-text and final replay-validation findings were resolved. The required repository lint-catalog review reported no findings before publication.

Handoff snapshot at `2026-09-05T05:32:27Z`, draft head `88b2fd7efd9d5cf7080033429acaea3b2d6e94e7`: five checks succeeded, seven were running, one was pending, and twelve were skipped. One earlier [label-policy check failed](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/33947430715/job/101255964965) because its push event preceded the `agentic-lint` label update; the [subsequent label-triggered check passed](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/33947441411/job/101255994500). The title, bodies, labels, exact head, and draft state were read back. Local rendering services were stopped. No continuing draft monitoring was started.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Both attempts of the 2026-09-02 ragged hero deployment (#8870) hung and produced fifteen minutes of complete silence: no error from NCCL, XLA, CUDA, the allocator or Kubernetes, and no artifact that survived the pod. The root cause is still open, but the investigation turned up five *separate* places where the information needed to diagnose it existed in principle and was simply never collected. Each is small, independent of the others, and independent of reproducing the hang; none of them is specific to the ragged transport, so all five pay off for any future silent stall.

Filing them together because they share one theme and because none is big enough to deserve its own issue. They can land as five small PRs in any order.

## 1. Iris never populates the GPU telemetry columns

`IrisTaskStat` declares `accelerator_util_pct` and `accelerator_mem_bytes` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/stats/tables.py:163`), `build_task_stat` takes both as keyword arguments (`tables.py:393`), and the tests cover them (`lib/iris/tests/cluster/stats/test_tables.py:123`). The producer never passes them: `TaskAttempt._emit_task_stat` builds its `ResourceUsage` from CPU, memory, disk and process count only and calls `build_task_stat` with no accelerator arguments (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/task_attempt.py:1020`). Both columns are therefore null for every task on every job.

This is the cheapest change here and the one with the most diagnostic value. During attempt 0's hang window both fields were null in all 2,636 samples. GPU utilisation on its own separates "spinning inside a resident kernel" from "the kernel never launched", which is the first branch any analysis of a silent hang has to take, and it needs no core dump, no rebuilt wheel and no reproduction. The same rows reproduced the known CPU signature exactly (the stuck rack at 4.04 cores against 7.85 elsewhere), so the nulls are a collection gap and not a query artifact.

There is already an `nvidia-smi` probe in the worker to build on (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/env_probe.py:139`), though it is one-shot at startup and queries `name,memory.total` only. The one real design question is per-task attribution: these nodes run four tasks each with one GPU apiece, so the sample has to be mapped to the task's own device, via `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,used_gpu_memory` or the task's device assignment rather than a node-wide average.

## 2. Enabling the progress diagnostic silently disables the watchdog on every other process

`ProgressWatchdogConfig.create` returns `None` for the *entire watchdog* whenever `diagnostic_timeout` is set and `process_index != 0` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/callbacks/progress_watchdog.py:211`). The intent was clearly to run the diagnostic capture only on process 0, but the early return drops the step, process and startup timeouts along with it. So switching the stall capture on costs you progress watchdogs on 175 of 176 processes, which is the opposite of what anyone enabling it wants, and it fails silently.

Fix is to gate only the diagnostic callback, not the watchdog itself. No behaviour change when `diagnostic_timeout` is unset, which is every configuration in the tree today. Roughly five lines plus a regression test.

## 3. The grug stall diagnostic is never wired, and the startup grace covers the hang

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py:938` calls `trainer.progress_watchdog.create(process_index=jax.process_index())` and passes no `diagnostic=`, so `diagnostic_timeout` stays unset and the stall-triggered verbose NCCL RAS capture publishes nothing. That capture is exactly what would have named the stuck ranks and the pending collective in both attempts; instead the only rank-level view we have is the periodic sample that happened to be running. Item 2 should land first, or wiring this here takes the watchdog away from 175 processes.

Separately, `_DEFAULT_STARTUP_GRACE_PERIOD` is one hour (`progress_watchdog.py:20`), which covered the whole of attempt 1's hang. That run was killed by hand, not by the watchdog. `1f0772d146` on `mcwitt/8870-repro` already shortens it for the hero ladder.

## 4. `CUDA_` environment variables cannot reach a training gang

`_FORWARDED_ENV_PREFIXES` in `experiments/grug/dispatch.py:29` is `("XLA_", "LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS", "NCCL_", "JAX_", "MALLOC_")`. `CUDA_` is absent, so none of the GPU core-dump variables can be forwarded to the tasks at all.

That matters more than it looks, because the CUDA driver reads those variables **once at process start**. There is no way to arm a core dump on a job that is already hung, and a hang raises no exception so `CUDA_ENABLE_COREDUMP_ON_EXCEPTION` never fires either. It is arm-at-launch or nothing. A dump taken from a stuck rank names the resident kernel and yields a per-block state table, which for this failure class is the whole ballgame: the LSA barrier is indexed by `blockIdx.x`, so that table names the diverged slots directly.

Adding the prefix is forwarding only and sets no defaults, so it costs nothing when unused. `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` needs excluding at the same time so a submitter-side value cannot override the runtime's device assignment. `f3600f88be` on `mcwitt/8870-repro` does both.

## 5. The state sharding dump dies with the pod

`hero_recipe.py:92` leaves `sharding_dump_path=None`, and the fallback is `default_grug_sharding_dump_path(log_dir, run_id)` = `log_dir / run_id / "artifacts" / ...` (`experiments/grug/sharding_dump.py:51-56`), which is pod-local. The hung run's dump was written and then lost with the pod.

Pointing it at the run's output path instead makes it survive, which is what would let a multi-rack dump be diffed against a single-rack one — the direct test for a sharding that JAX infers differently at different scales, and one that needs no special build. Six lines; `af282dcbe8` on `mcwitt/8870-repro` does it.

## Deliberately not in scope

The #8861 fix (the step counter's inferred sharding, `6406302890` + `2819d33bf6` on `mcwitt/8870-repro`) is a correctness fix with a determined root cause, not a diagnostic, and it should go straight to its own PR against #8861 rather than be bundled here.

The diagnostic PJRT wheel (`marin-community/xla` branch `mcwitt/8870-barrier-timeout`, built as `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-ca0716a2da95`) is not free: it moves `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION` from 2.29.7 to the 2.30.7 the runtime actually loads, which changes the headers the device kernels compile against. It belongs to the #8870 hunt and needs a single-rack smoke of its own.

## Done when

All five have landed on main, and a future silent stall on a grug gang leaves behind: GPU utilisation per task, a progress watchdog on every process, a rank-level RAS capture triggered by the stall, an armed core-dump pipe, and a sharding dump that outlives the pod.

Context and evidence for every claim above: #8870.

comments.author: ClassicLarry

This behavior seems concerning. Attention is basically inactive on layer0. 🤖 Layer-skip ablation on the step-42k checkpoint — dropless macro loss with whole transformer layers dropped from the forward (restored on one rack, scored with the hero's own dropless evaluator).

| ablation | layers run | dropless macro loss | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| baseline | all 48 | 2.093 | — |
| skip first 10 | 10–47 | 6.584 | +4.49 (3.1×) |

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Summarizing findings:
1. At hero_scale attention gate shows uncharacteristic increase in norm. 
2. The 48 heads of the attention gate show high cosine similarity on any given layer. Checking layer zero, 98 percent of the time the attention gate is driving attention down to under 5 percent of its initial output scale.
3. Contributions to the residual stream scale with layer depth. MLP tends to contribute about 2x more than attention. Layer zero contributes about 1/10 the norm of the initial embed. Layer 48 contributes about 10x the norm of the initial embed. 
4. However zeroing out attention on the first 10 layers causes a meaningful increase in loss. A greater increase (2x) than zeroing out attention on the last 10 layers. So attention in early layers is still contributing very meaningfully. (changes from attention in early layers influence what updates later layers make). This contribution should act as a 'tether' that prevents these layers from becoming useless. (the gradient would yell very loudly if attention gate turned them off completely). Main learning: output scale does not correspond to impact.

Suspicion is that the attn_gate parameter has been co-opted in early layers to function as an output scaling mechanism. The intention was for the input RMSNorm on the attn block to handle this, or the sconv on attn_out.

Given that the first 10 attn layers are still critical and actively getting used (just smaller scale outputs), not viewing as issue that requires immediate action. Things would prompt intervention:
1. Loss curve slows down and no longer beats projection.
2. Ablating removing early attention layers actually shows no impact on loss later on in training.
3. We get positive results from an ablation on 1 rack that resumes from checkpoint, when compared to baseline:

Ablation ideas:
1. Update attention gate from v = 2*sigmoid(x)*v to v = (0.05 + 2*sigmoid(x))*v. Give nonzero floor.
2. Instead of hardcoded 0.05, make it a learnable bias per head with very high beta1 and beta2. Init to 0.
3. Add a general output scalar on each attn output. Init to 1 with very high beta1 and beta2.
4. Add some regularization to attn gate weight (weight decay).
5. Add hardcoded bias that ramps per step from 0 to 0.05 over 1000 steps.

All of these ablation ideas would probably not be effective as-is. But testing on 1 rack would give signal and better intuition on how the system is behaving. Since attention gate runs through a sigmoid, it would never fully decay to zero. Since this dynamic only occurs on hero scale (48 layers), all ablations would need to occur there.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Main initial concern here was that gradient signal to the attention matrices would be getting killed by attn gate being off. But actually, the gradient signal is likely still reasonable, its just that model has adopted a behavior where output scale grows with depth (but early layers still impact prediction heavily through their impact on subsequent layers), and this depth scaling is managed partially by the attention gate, perhaps partially because matrices are under hyperball. Will be important to get per-layer gradient logging on Hero to track this more actively. (scan layers is bundling the gradient across all layers).

Traditionally the intent of residual highway is it gives direct gradient signal back from lm_head to every layer directly. However since we see output scale of every layer increase, the early layers will influence prediction very little through direct residual highway. Instead, their influence comes from how they influence subsequent layers. This seems like it would perhaps be less stable. Though training seems extremely stable so far? As long as gradient on attention matrices in initial layers looks ok, then biasing towards no action.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Layer-0 headwise attention gate, per-vocab-token (step-42000). The gate is `2·sigmoid(attn_in @ attn_gate)`, one value per head (48 heads); at layer 0 `attn_in` is a deterministic function of the token embedding, so each token has a fixed 48-head gate vector. "On" = gate > 1 (i.e. `attn_in @ attn_gate > 0`).

Layer-0 attention is near-closed by default: mean gate over the whole vocab is **0.013**. Only **546 of 128,256 tokens open ≥1 head**, and just **93 open all 48**. The tokens that stay on fall into three buckets:

**1. Reserved/special tokens (128000–128255)** — the bulk. ~200 of the 256 special tokens open all 48 heads (opensum 96/96): `<|reserved_special_token_*|>` plus the structural specials (`<|begin_of_text|>`, `<|end_of_text|>`, `<|eot_id|>`).

**2. Malformed / byte-fragment real-vocab tokens** — the top non-special tokens are almost all junk:
- undecodable UTF-8 byte fragments that decode to `�` (ids 124, 125, 178–187), several at the full 96/96
- rare foreign-script subwords: Turkish (`ıldığında`, `ılmaz`, `uştur`, `ılmaktadır`), Cyrillic/Ukrainian (`уватися`, `илася`, `аракт`), Czech (`ujícím`), CJK spam strings (`菲律宾申博`, `갤로그로`)
- gibberish/spam: `eoqkrvldkf`, `.:.:.:.:.:.:`, `.**************`, `ЎыџN`

**3. Ordinary English text tokens** — essentially none; common words sit at gate ≈ 0.

Distribution of open-head counts (real-vocab tokens only, excluding the special block): 345 open ≥1 head, 32 open ≥12 heads.

🤖 d1024 weight-decay ablation — final (all three finished at step 15,276; 32 H100, batch 2048; dropless eval). wd schedule on the targeted leaves: 0 for the first 15% of training, then the 0.05·(1−step/N) line (0.0425 at the 15% mark) decaying to 0. Same seed; differ only in the decay target.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 attn_gate logit scaling — dropless eval on the step-48000 hero checkpoint (d6144, 1 rack, expert-collapsed dropless mesh, 50 batches × 64 seq per paloma tag).

Applies a scalar multiplier to the headwise attn_gate logits before the sigmoid: `gate = 2·sigmoid(scale · (x @ attn_gate))`. `scale<1` shrinks the logits toward 0, relaxing every head's gate toward the neutral 1.0; `scale=0` removes the learned headwise gating entirely (all gates = 1.0).

| attn_gate logit scale | dropless macro loss |
|---|---|
| 1.0 (baseline) | 2.0875 |
| 0.8 | 2.0973 |
| 0.6 | 2.7852 |
| 0.4 | 8.4599 |
| 0.2 | 9.8986 |
| 0.0 | 9.3836 |

Shrinking the gate logits by 20% is nearly free (+0.010). The model degrades at 0.6 and collapses at 0.4 and below — the learned headwise gating is load-bearing, and its effect is concentrated in the top ~40% of the logit magnitude. (The 0.2 < 0.0 non-monotonicity is inside the already-collapsed regime.)

Caveat: the `paloma/macro_loss` sub-aggregate came back `nan` for every ablation including the unaltered baseline, so it's an eval-set aggregation artifact unrelated to the scaling; the table reports the overall dropless macro across all resolved eval tags.

So see very little downside to starting with a more conservative 0.03 WD, then ramping later if needed.

comments.author: Mooler0410
comments.body: This might be related to what we found in our ultra-sparse MoE training (768 experts / top-8, 60B and 180B); the write-up is here: [https://alltoall.notion.site/save-lower-layer-moe-experts-llal](https://alltoall.notion.site/save-lower-layer-moe-experts-llal) In our runs the routed experts of the **first few MoE layers stop learning** after a few thousand steps, while the shared expert stays healthy and loss / evals / load balance all look normal. We trained with AdamW, weight decay and the default ε, so it showed up as weight-norm collapse in those layers. With Muon, or with a very small ε, the norms look fine but the layers still stop learning (momentum in those layers drops ~3 orders of magnitude, and masking their routed experts barely changes downstream metrics) — unless we give them an extra informative signal during a critical period at the start of training (an aux LM loss on the first MoE layer for the first 2–4k steps). Alongside this we saw the early-layer attention stop learning too, which makes sense: if the MLP stops adding meaningful representation to the residual, there is nothing stable for attention to build on. In our runs the order was clearly MLP first, attention as a consequence. Your setup is very different from ours (MuonH with hyperball, latent MoE, headwise attention gates, QB, no dense layers), so we're only saying this might be the same thing. **We also don't know what happens at 18T tokens — our longest run in this blog is 2T, and there every collapsed layer except the first MoE layer had either recovered or was starting to by the end; the first one stayed dead.** What you are seeing in layer 0 — attention gated shut for essentially every ordinary token, diverging from the ladder at ~1% into the run — looks like the attention side of the same thing. And in the per-layer watch from ra2a-evaldl-c3f51 (48k checkpoint) we also see the abnormally small gradients on the **layer-0/1 routed experts: w_gate/w_up/w_down at 2.4e-5 / 2.4e-5 / 6.0e-5 in layer 0, 200–430× below layers 5–19 and ~100× below the layer-0 shared expert,** while the shared experts and attention in the same layer are normal; layer 1 is ~10× low, layers 2–4 look fine. One cheap check would settle it: **routed-expert-only masking (probably free ? ).**

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: > This might be related to what we found in our ultra-sparse MoE training (768 experts / top-8, 60B and 180B); the write-up is here: https://alltoall.notion.site/save-lower-layer-moe-experts-llal Great blog! I think our early attention layers are still learning fine, just using a somewhat awkward mechanism (the attention gate) to manage their scale. But what you found- the dead gradient in first 2 layers, does probably indicate those routed experts are not contributing. Updated grads: I love your idea of starting training with a temporary aux loss. At this stage, I think interventions midrun are probably not worthwhile for those 2 layers. Doubling the number of routed parameters is equivalent to the gain of training on 20% more tokens, when measured near compute optimal. So losing 2 layers of routed experts, (4% of routed params), is probably very marginal impact on model quality (part of this is also because we have atypically large shared experts). But maybe after the pretrain run we could just remove them, or try some experiments on intermittent checkpoints for science purposes.

issues.title: Hero Run: Attn Gate Norm Growth

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Four `long-context/*` branches implement the context-parallel gaps #8374 lists for Grug main: a `context` mesh axis, context-sharded queries in the production FA4/CuTe attention path, a token-axis policy for MoE routing and loss under a sharded sequence, and an opt-in Transformer Engine CP backend. An integration branch composed them and trained the hero shape at sequence 262144 on one NVL72 rack (EP16xCP4, global batch 16, 4.19M tokens/step) from the hero's step-6000 checkpoint: 8.78% MFU, 113.5 s/step, peak HBM 127.6 of 138.2 GiB, and a drop fraction of 18% that was still rising. The hero's 1.15/1.15 capacity factors, tuned at sequence 4096 with batch 1024, do not carry to 262K at batch 16.

## Description

The 535B-A23B campaign (#8435) plans context extensions to 65K and possibly 262K; #8374 tracks the blockers and names four gaps in Grug main. Each gap has its own branch with a spec, implementation, an independent code review, and a fix round; specs and implementation notes live under `.agents/projects/` on each branch.

* [`long-context/mesh-context-axis`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/mesh-context-axis): `(replica_dcn, data, context, expert, model)` compact mesh via `compact_grug_mesh(context_axis_size=...)`, ported from the finished 262K TPU CP4 run (commit `b2cf4fe1aa` on `june_tpu_67b_a2b`). Checkpoints record no mesh, so pre-context checkpoints restore onto the 5-axis mesh unchanged.
* [`long-context/fa4-sequence-sharding`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/fa4-sequence-sharding): all-gather-KV context parallelism in the FA4/CuTe path. A runtime `q_offset` kernel input supplies the causal frontier (the kernel derives it from the local query index), the shard_map transpose provides the dK/dV psum over `context`, and the backward query-tile range is clamped to close an out-of-bounds LSE/dPsum read for key CTAs past a shard's queries. 19/19 GPU tests on GB200 at seq 512 / cp 2, including the hero tile config.
* [`long-context/moe-context-sharding`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/moe-context-sharding): the flattened token axis is sharded over `("replica_dcn", "data", "expert", "context")` and each context shard routes its tokens independently; EP drop psums, both QB estimators, and the fused cross-entropy loss reduce over spec-derived token axes.
* [`long-context/te-cp-backend`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/te-cp-backend): opt-in `gpu_te_cp` backend whose striping matches TE v2.17's `reorder_causal_striped` source. Runtime is blocked by the cuDNN `BAD_PARAM` in #8141, and no shipped variant can select it yet: a homogeneous layer scan cannot give TE a static per-layer window.
* [`long-context/262k-rack-experiment`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/long-context/262k-rack-experiment): merges the four, ports the bench launcher flags (`--seq-len`, `--restore-from`, `--context-axis-size`, `--expert-axis-size`, `--qk-mult`), and adds what composition required: composite `("expert", "context")` parameter sharding, a context-sharded residual stream, a left-halo `short_conv` wrapper, and a `MeshConfig` fix for global batch below the device count.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure whether the hero shape trains at 262144 sequence length on GB200 and what it costs in memory, throughput, and routing drops from a real checkpoint. This covers gates 1-2 of the early-cooldown list and the docs-per-shard routing risk #8374 calls the unresolved model-quality question.

## Status

Probe complete. Run `lc262k-ep16cp4-08251450` restored the 535B step-6000 checkpoint in 3.5 minutes and trained to the 6100 stop step on one rack; the job sealed `succeeded` with one preemption. Steady state over steps 6000-6012, from raw timestamps: 113.5 s/step, 37,042 tokens/s, 8.78% MFU, peak HBM 127.63 GiB against a 138.22 GiB limit, loss 1.416 median.

`moe/drop_fraction` was 0.18 median (0.081 sender, 0.101 receiver), rising 0.168 to 0.207 over the window. `capacity_overflow_rate_mean` tracks it exactly, so the loss is capacity clipping, not transport. Baselines: 3.5% drops on the live 4K hero, 1.7e-4 on the 4K one-rack restore arm. At batch 16 each expert coordinate routes one 65,536-token document instead of sixteen independent 4,096-token sequences, and expert load within one document is correlated enough that the fixed per-expert capacity clips it.

Caveat: the LR heuristic reads `HERO_MODEL.max_seq_len` (4096), so the probe applied ~6.9e-5, about 2% of the checkpoint's rate. The run measures throughput, memory, and routing; it does not diagnose 262K training stability.

## Links

* Plan and full run record (three failed attempts and their fixes): [`.agents/projects/20260824_262k_rack_experiment.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/long-context/262k-rack-experiment/.agents/projects/20260824_262k_rack_experiment.md)
* W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc262k-ep16cp4-08251450
* Blocker tracker: #8374. TE/cuDNN toolchain: #8141. Hero campaign: #8435.

## Decision Log

* All-gather-KV FA4 is the production CP path; TE stays an opt-in seam until the #8141 toolchain is fixed.
* Parameters, their fp32 pinned-host masters, and Muon state shard over composite `("expert", "context")` so CP does not multiply per-rank optimizer memory; without this, EP16xCP4 needs ~1072 GB/node of host memory against ~850 available. Muon's Newton-Schulz derives its layout from the parameter instead of a hard-coded spec.
* The residual stream is context-sharded end to end, unblocked by a `kernel_size - 1` left halo (carrying neighbour segment ids) above the unchanged `short_conv` Pallas kernel. This took the rack step from an uncompilable 350 GiB/device to 127.6 GiB, and the d768 ladder at seq 262144 / cp4 from 19.71 to 13.59 GiB.
* `--schedule-steps 4470000` holds the mixture's simulated-epoching budget at ratio ~1 so no cell slices empty at sequence 262144.

## Conclusion

The hero shape compiles, restores, and trains at 262K on one rack with 10.6 GiB of HBM headroom. Routing capacity is the open problem: 18% of assignments drop under the 4K-tuned capacity factors, and the rate was still rising when the probe ended.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Marin has no way to mark a test as needing a GPU, a minimum device count, or a specific accelerator. Some accelerator tests skip invisibly in CI as a result, and the two that need real device topology were written outside pytest entirely.

`tests/test_utils.py` provides `skip_if_no_tpu` and nothing equivalent for GPUs or device counts. The root `pyproject.toml` markers are `slow`, `integration`, `data_integration`, `cluster`, `requires_cluster`, `docker`, and `manual`; none describes hardware. `tests/cluster/conftest.py` names two clusters, `MARIN_TPU_CLUSTER` and `MARIN_GPU_CLUSTER = "cw-us-east-02a"`, with no entry for the GB200 cluster `cw-us-east-08a`.

Two tests in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py` check the ragged all-to-all MoE backend against a dense reference and run nowhere:

```
uv run python -m pytest lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py -rs -k "ragged or granular or clip"
...
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[ragged_all_to_all]
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_reports_positive_drop_count_in_ragged_a2a_when_over_capacity
5 passed, 2 skipped
```

They skip on `requires an even number of >=2 devices`, and forcing two CPU devices hits the next guard, `ragged_all_to_all is not implemented on XLA:CPU`. Every job in `.github/workflows/` runs on `ubuntu-latest`. The five that pass cover lowering, offset arithmetic against a NumPy simulation of the collective, and capacity clipping in isolation. None runs the real collective or the SM100 expert kernels.

The root `addopts` does not include `-rs`, so these skips never appear in CI output. A green run with full coverage and a green run with no ragged coverage look identical.

Both files that need real accelerator topology avoided pytest. `lib/iris/tests/e2e/gpu_gang_smoke.py` is a standalone `__main__` script with `--target kind|coreweave` and `--i-understand-the-cost`; it mock-labels kind nodes to simulate an NVLink domain instead of requiring one. `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ragged_ep_check.py` (PR #8549) submits a 4-GPU GB200 job, computes a pass/fail verdict, and raises on failure, but sits under `experiments/` with no scheduled caller.

Two cases need different mechanisms. A test like the levanter one needs N local devices inside the pytest process. A test like `ragged_ep_check` needs no local hardware: it submits a job whose constraint rides in `ResourceConfig.with_gpu("GB200", count=4, ...)`, so what it needs is a cluster fixture and a way to declare that the run is expensive.

#7242 delivered `tests/cluster/`, the `cluster` marker, and `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` for smokes that submit real jobs. It left open which hardware a test needs and what a test that cannot get that hardware should do.

Done when:

- A test can declare a local device requirement and skip with a named reason instead of an ad-hoc in-file guard.
- Skipped tests are visible in CI output.
- A job-submitting test can target the GB200 cluster through a fixture, and its cost is expressible on the test rather than only in the workflow.
- One existing case is ported as the reference: the levanter ragged EP tests, or `ragged_ep_check.py`.

It says `tests/cluster/` "covers submitting a job to a standing cluster" and that the gap is a GB200 lane and a cost tier on the existing workflow. The workflow no longer exists. #8605 deleted `.github/workflows/marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` on 2026-08-22, and its commit message gives the reason:

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting my comment above, which was too absolute. "No workflow runs the `cluster` marker" is accurate; "accelerator tests have no automated vehicle" was not.

Scheduled GPU work does run. `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` fires daily at 10:00 UTC against `cw-us-west-04a`, sets `CANARY_ACCELERATOR: gpu`, and runs `python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry` on 8x H100 through Iris, with `scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py` asserting the result. That is a real accelerator smoke on a daily cron. It is not pytest and carries no marker.

`iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` looks like a second GPU lane and is not one. It runs `pytest tests/test_integration_test.py -m integration` on PRs touching `lib/iris/**`, and the workflow comment says it submits "against the shared H100" — but the jobs `tests/integration_test.py` submits are `ResourceConfig.with_cpu()` with `require_accelerator=False`. It exercises a CoreWeave-hosted controller, not a GPU.

The deleted `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` had two jobs, not one. `marin-tpu-smokes` ran on the schedule; `marin-gpu-smokes` was `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.run_gpu`, so it never ran on a cron at all. The 38 timed-out scheduled runs the deleting commit cites were the TPU job. Standing-cluster GPU tests were therefore never automatic, before or after #8605.

So the gap this issue describes is sharper than "no runner": **no pytest marker anywhere selects GPU work.** The `cluster` marker has no workflow, and the `integration` marker runs only CPU jobs. Every GPU assertion in CI today lives in the canary ferry, outside pytest.

Two facts worth having when someone picks this up. The canary already parameterizes the accelerator (`CANARY_GPU_TYPE`, documented as "H100, GH200, B200", plus `CANARY_GPU_COUNT` and `CANARY_GPU_REPLICAS`), so scheduling GPU work of a given shape from Actions is solved machinery rather than something to build. And `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` and `iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` share the concurrency group `iris-coreweave-ci-shared` because they contend for one host, so any added lane needs a capacity story and not only a config entry.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Build RiffleEval as a paired long-context evaluation of coherent stream tracking. Each base item keeps the source text, question, answer, distractors, and token budget fixed while changing document chunks from blocked to riffled order. The primary result is the per-item riffle penalty, sliced by foreign-chunk interference count and token distance.

UncheatableEval is a candidate source feed after revision pinning, token-length filtering, license review, and safety filtering. Its current Marin integration is unsuitable: it downloads a stale GitHub fork whose records are capped at 5,000 characters and supplies no questions or evidence annotations. For v0, use frozen natural documents with exact-answer factual overlays; evaluate a filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` subset as one source arm, beginning with English Wikipedia and permissively licensed documents.

## Description

Long-context evaluations such as NIAH often test retrieval of one conspicuous item from a large context. RiffleEval tests whether a model can maintain several ordered information streams whose chunks repeatedly alternate across a 32K–64K prompt, then reconstruct facts within one stream.

For source document \(D_i = [C_{i,1}, \ldots, C_{i,n}]\), generate a legal merge that preserves chunk order within each source. Every chunk receives an opaque, per-example stream ID and ordinal. Questions and evidence annotations are created and verified against the clean document before riffling.

Each base item produces these conditions:

1. Clean target document, for source-task competence.
2. Blocked full context, with the target and distractor documents contiguous.
3. Riffled full context, with identical content and prompt budget.
4. Adjacent-evidence control for multi-evidence items.

The v0 task families are single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration. Cross-stream joins and continuation NLL remain follow-ups.

The proposed context-length and stream-count matrix is not a full Cartesian product. With 4K–8K source documents, 32K supports roughly 4–8 streams and 64K supports roughly 8–16 streams. Larger documents or additional filler semantics would be required to hold stream count fixed while scaling total context. The generator must reject infeasible cells instead of silently repeating or padding sources.

## Hypothesis or Goal

At fixed content and question difficulty, riffling causes a measurable accuracy loss beyond the loss caused by the same blocked distractors. The loss increases with the number of intervening foreign chunks after controlling for absolute token distance. Better long-context checkpoints should move the retention curve toward larger interference counts.

## Status

Background research is complete. No implementation or model run has started.

### Proposed v0

- 250–500 verified base items, expanded into deterministic paired variants.
- 32K and 64K contexts; feasible 4/8/16-stream cells; approximately 512-token chunks.
- Exact short answers with one-evidence and two-evidence overlays.
- Opaque opening and closing markers with tokenizer-balanced random IDs.
- Random and same-domain distractors.
- Native-model score with tools disabled.
- Exact match, per-item riffle penalty, blocked-to-riffled penalty, and retention curves by token distance, interference count, evidence count, and active streams.
- Target-stream extraction and oracle-evidence diagnostics to separate stream selection from reasoning.
- Frozen generator version, seed, source revision/hash, tokenizer, prompt, and structural metadata for every item.

### UncheatableEval corpus decision

Use it as an optional source-discovery and freshness feed. Do not use the published collection as the sole corpus or reuse `experiments/datasets/uncheatable.py`.

The current upstream `-Long` snapshots contain 7,500 records across 15 categories and retain source URL, date, category, `content`, and `untruncated_content`. They provide recent natural interference, but no question, answer, stable ID, evidence span, or hop graph. The dataset card declares no dataset license, and source rights differ by document. AO3 has safety concerns; arbitrary GitHub files need license and secret checks; BBC is a poor redistribution default; PDF extraction can corrupt arXiv text. Freshness only protects models whose training cutoff predates the crawl.

A derived arm must:

- pin the Hugging Face revision and content hash;
- filter on benchmark-tokenizer length, language, quality, and safety;
- record URL, collection date, source category, license, and transformed-text hash;
- begin with English Wikipedia and individually cleared permissive sources;
- exclude BBC and AO3 from v0;
- generate exact-answer overlays and frozen evidence spans against the exact transformed text.

## Background Research Brief

- Effort / stop rule / date: medium; 2026-08-24; stopped when the internal, benchmark, corpus, and contradiction passes no longer changed the v0 recommendation.

### Current Marin context

- #7638 owns RULER integration. RiffleEval should not duplicate its eval harness work.
- #4736 specified the closest reusable data contract: frozen long-document QA items with exact answers, evidence spans, and length bins.
- #7181 found that retained MRCR context reduced final-turn PPL from 21.0855 to 10.4012 at 8,192 tokens. Its extraction PR #7203 closed unmerged, so it is prior evidence rather than current infrastructure.
- #5825 previously built 32K/64K long-document PPL slices; the implementation was later removed by #6633.
- No existing issue or implementation tests repeated switching among several coherent streams.

### External prior art

- [RULER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654) varies context length and task complexity across multi-needle retrieval, variable tracking, aggregation, and QA. RiffleEval adds coherent natural streams and a paired blocked/riffled intervention.
- [MRCR/Michelangelo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) shows that repeated, similar requests and ordinal selection are harder than unique needles. RiffleEval should include similar competing streams and report random/noise floors.
- [NoLiMa](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167) shows that lexical overlap makes retrieval easier and normalizes long-context scores to short-context competence. RiffleEval should vary lexical overlap and reject items with weak clean-document accuracy.
- [BABILong](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf) distributes multi-fact synthetic tasks through natural books. RiffleEval adds several foreground streams, explicit stream identities, and the same task before and after structural transformation.
- [LOFT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121) found that marker and prompt formatting materially affect retrieval. Marker tokenization and query placement must be fixed or explicitly ablated.
- [UncheatableEval](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval) evaluates rolling internet text by NLL. Its freshness method is useful for source discovery; it does not provide RiffleEval annotations.

### Contradiction and shortcut pass

- Random riffles and IDs prevent fixed-order contamination but do not prevent a model from answering public facts from parametric memory. Synthetic counterfactual overlays provide the durable control.
- Opaque IDs expose segmentation but do not prevent keyword search within the target stream. Lexical-overlap and near-neighbor distractor slices remain necessary.
- “Uniform-ish” legal merges do not independently control gap length. Sample examples from explicit interference-count and token-distance strata.
- Marker token lengths can differ across tokenizers and become an unplanned treatment. Balance marker encodings and store their token counts.
- Native QA generation from unannotated documents can admit one-passage shortcuts. Require evidence spans, clean-document verification, and minimal-evidence ablations.

### Recommended next experiments

#### 1. Validate the paired structural signal at 32K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: 100 overlay items, four streams, 512-token chunks; clean, blocked, and riffled conditions on two representative models with different long-context capability.
- Expected signal / falsifier: a nonzero blocked-to-riffled penalty that grows across interference buckets while clean accuracy remains high. Near-zero penalty, floor-level clean accuracy, or prompt-format sensitivity larger than the treatment falsifies the current setup.

#### 2. Add two-evidence integration and 64K

- Minimum experiment / baseline: two controlled facts in widely separated chunks; adjacent-evidence and oracle-extracted-stream baselines; feasible 8/16-stream cells.
- Expected signal / falsifier: two-evidence retention degrades faster than one-evidence retention while oracle extraction recovers most accuracy. Failure of the oracle indicates base reasoning or question-construction problems.

#### 3. Compare source pools

- Minimum experiment / baseline: matched overlays over a pinned filtered UncheatableEval `-Long` arm and one stable, license-cleared long-document corpus.
- Expected signal / falsifier: model ranking and riffle penalty remain stable across source pools. Large domain-specific reversals require a multi-corpus benchmark or removal of the unstable source.

### Source ledger

| Source | Type | Location | Claim used for | Confidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RULER | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654 | complexity axes and baselines | high | nearest variable-tracking precedent |
| Michelangelo / MRCR | paper and official code | https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640 | repeated similar needles and order | high | conversation format differs from riffled documents |
| NoLiMa | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167 | lexical-overlap shortcut and retention normalization | high | single-association retrieval |
| BABILong | paper | https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/c0d62e70dbc659cc9bd44cbcf1cb652f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf | distributed multi-fact reasoning in natural text | high | one background stream |
| LOFT | paper | https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13121 | formatting and identifier sensitivity | high | fixed retrieval corpora |
| UncheatableEval | official repo and dataset | https://huggingface.co/datasets/Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07-Long | source schema, freshness, and corpus limitations | high | no dataset-level license or QA annotations |
| Marin #4736 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4736 | QA manifest and evidence schema | high | closed before implementation |
| Marin #7638 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7638 | active RULER scope | high | avoid duplicate harness work |
| Marin #7181 | GitHub issue | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7181 | paired MRCR PPL result | high | extraction PR closed unmerged |

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates: #7638, #4736, #7181, #5825

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-24: scope v0 to paired single-stream exact QA and two-evidence within-stream integration at 32K/64K.
- 2026-08-24: treat UncheatableEval as an optional filtered source arm; reject the current Marin handle and the unfiltered published corpus as the canonical benchmark source.
- 2026-08-24: defer cross-stream joins, continuation NLL, and 128K+ until the primary structural signal is validated.

## Conclusion

Open. Advance to implementation if the 32K pilot produces high clean accuracy, a reproducible blocked-to-riffled penalty, and a stable ordering across source pools and marker templates.
