comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖

Reproduction of the audit: I re-ran a seeded sample of the audited rows independently (the audit's scripts were read, not executed). Rows from `nvidia/Nemotron-SFT-Competitive-Programming-v2` at Marin's pinned revision `778afc98`, joined to the audit's per-row lists at `Min-Li/marin-sft-data-audit` `d2cb335e`; official tests from `open-r1/codeforces` `fbe3f6e9`. Sample: 100 claimed failures + 100 claimed-pass controls per category (seed `20261117`), re-run on isolated CPU jobs in `us-east-02a` with no network access during execution; untrusted code never ran outside the sandbox. Toolchain matched the audit's judging conditions where practical: g++ 13.3.0 (the audit's judge compiler), CPython 3.13.18 + PyPy 3.10.16, PostgreSQL 18.7 (the audit's engine version), MySQL 8.4.13 (default and relaxed sql_mode passes), SQLite 3.40.1 (the audit used 3.46.1 on its first engine; recorded as residual drift). Every C++/Python code extraction reproduced the audit's published `code_sha1`.

Results (claimed-failure reproduction / control confirmation):

| Category | Fails reproduced | Controls confirmed | Decision (≥90% / ≥95% bars) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ compile | 100/100 | 100/100 | reproduce → recommend dropping the failing rows |
| C++ official tests | 100/100 | 100/100 | reproduce → recommend dropping |
| Python official tests | 100/100 | 100/100 | reproduce → recommend dropping |
| text_to_sql execution | 100/100 | 100/100 | reproduce → recommend dropping |
| text_to_sql schema-not-loaded | 100/100 | 100/100 | reproduce → recommend dropping |

No disagreements remained in the final run: the only initial divergences were environment-side (PostgreSQL contrib-extension and MySQL sql_mode ladder passes, which the audit's own multi-engine ladder also applies), and they resolved once those passes were mirrored. Caveats carry over from the audit itself: its failure rates are lower bounds with relaxed time limits, the `time_limit` slice of the test-failure lists is the most machine-dependent, and dropping rows shifts the difficulty mix. `schema_not_loaded` is not wired in PR #11546; reproducing it supports adding it.

Full numbers, per-row reproduction results, drop lists (uuid + reason + contributor receipt SHA + reproduction receipt SHA) and receipts: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-audit-repro/runs/20261117-063043/` — [Filer link](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fsft-audit-repro%2Fruns%2F20261117-063043). The next-mix owner has been handed the lists.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Concurrent SkyRL jobs can start on the same Iris host. Some Ray services require a concrete TCP port before the service binds it. Two launchers can choose the same free port during that interval, even when their pods have separate filesystems. PR #12313 holds a host-network lease for those listeners in `vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/ray_ports.py`.

Move the lease primitive into Iris and make SkyRL call it. Keep the mapping of Ray services to their supported port modes in SkyRL. Explicit Iris allocations must still take precedence, and Ray services that accept a kernel-assigned port should still receive zero.

Cover two independent launchers sharing a network namespace. They should receive distinct ports while their leases overlap, skip occupied ports, and release their claims when the launcher exits, including after a crash.

[PR review requesting the follow-up](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12313#issuecomment-7180835193)

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

PR #12313 implements host-network leases in SkyRL's [`ray_ports.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7a1ae6ed8b3120862f3ac1f941d72284a65033e0/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/ray_ports.py#L36-L101). The generic candidate scan and abstract Unix socket claim sit beside Ray-specific port policy, so another Iris caller cannot reuse the claim. Iris's [`find_free_port`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2de6fcd77775426aecfc8c9c7c78cbc7db8a5d99/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/types.py#L70-L97) returns a port after closing its TCP probe; it does not hold a cross-process lease.

**Relevant code**
- [`ray_ports.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7a1ae6ed8b3120862f3ac1f941d72284a65033e0/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/ray_ports.py) — allocation and Ray policy
- [`task_runtime.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7a1ae6ed8b3120862f3ac1f941d72284a65033e0/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/task_runtime.py#L2387) — lease lifetime
- [`test_ray_ports.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7a1ae6ed8b3120862f3ac1f941d72284a65033e0/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/tests/test_ray_ports.py) — concurrent launcher coverage

# Proposed Fix

Move candidate selection and the socket lease into a public Iris runtime module. Have SkyRL request leases only for services requiring concrete ports, keep explicit Iris allocations and native zero modes unchanged, and hold the leases around Ray's lifetime. Add Iris tests using independent processes to check overlapping claims, occupied ports, release on normal exit, and release after a killed launcher. Stack the follow-up on #12313 until it merges.

spillover_issues.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
spillover_issues.body:
On a multi-user host, the first Iris caller creates `/tmp/iris` with the caller's umask. With umask `022`, the directory is `0755`, so another Unix user cannot write a port lock. [`reserve_free_port()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/bb97576da1dae7c6173cc6e85372d81950b5f8c0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/types.py#L81-L110) catches the write's `PermissionError` as `OSError`, skips all 1,000 ports, and raises `No free port found in range 10000-11000` even when ports are free. Kubernetes port-forward and GCP SSH tunnels both use this reservation.

Reproduce on a test host:
1. With `/tmp/iris` absent and umask `022`, have user A open and close an Iris tunnel.
2. Have a different Unix user open an Iris tunnel on the same host. The port scan reports no free port despite available ports.

Expected: Iris reserves and releases local ports across Unix users on the same host. If lock storage is inaccessible, report the permission error instead of false port exhaustion.

Found during [review of #11915](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11915#issuecomment-7231940629).
spillover_issues.title: [iris] Port locks fail across users when /tmp/iris is not writable

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
Snowball (67B-A2B) serving on TPU v4 with TP=8 fails during precompile: the MoE grouped-matmul kernel needs more VMEM than a v4 core has. This blocks the smallest slice that fits the weights (v4-16, 8 chips). Part of https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11855.

## Repro

- Model: `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05` @ `ac60d940`.
- Stack: marin PR 11780 plus PR 11781's tpu-inference pin `03f10d39` (vLLM `fb02daf1`).
- Command: `marin-serve iris <model> --cluster marin --tpu v4-16 --region us-central2 --no-preemptible --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 32768 --memory 300g --wait-timeout 3600`. `--no-preemptible` is added in the task/535 draft PR.
- Result: weights load. Then `_precompile_backbone_text_only` fails with:

```
RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: XLA:TPU compile permanent error. Ran out of memory in memory space vmem.
Used 16.22M of 16.00M vmem. Exceeded vmem capacity by 224.0K.
XLA label: gmm_v2-g_256-m_512-k_2560-act_silu-n_512-tm_512-tk_2560-tn_256
```

## Cause

`tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py`:
- `gmm` sets `vmem_limit_bytes` to 90% of VMEM capacity.
- `calculate_tiling` then grows `tile_m` in up to 4 buckets while `_gmm_vmem_estimate` stays under that limit.
- For these shapes, the estimate is about 14.7 MB (LHS 5.2 + RHS 7.9 + accumulator 1.0 + output 0.5). The compiled kernel uses 16.22 MB.
- The estimate leaves out the other scratch buffers, such as the zero-fill tile and the per-sublane output buffer, plus compiler scratch.
- A v4 core has 16 MiB of VMEM, so the gap overflows it. v5p and v6e have much larger VMEM, so they don't hit it.
- `tile_m` reaches 512 for any batch of 512 or more rows, so no serving flag avoids it.
- Upstream tpu-inference has since removed this local `gmm_v2` copy (commit `9dc239779`, "Remove the local copy of gmm v2"). That landed after our fork base `34535b11`.

## Options

1. **Serve on v4-32 with TP=16** (no code change). Each device then holds half of the expert matmul, so the same tiles need about 10–12 MB. This is the route that served Snowball on v4 in October. It is being tested now.
2. **Patch the fork's `calculate_tiling`** so v4-16 works. For example, count the missing scratch buffers in `_gmm_vmem_estimate`, or keep more headroom when VMEM is 16 MiB or less. This needs a fork PR, a Marin re-pin and the TPU release gate. A rebase onto upstream's tokamax kernel may also fix it; that is not checked.

## Decision needed

Whether v4-16 (8 chips) is worth option 2, or whether v4-32 (16 chips) is fine for the shared endpoint.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The fork's `calculate_tiling` budgets LHS, RHS, accumulator, and output tiles, but `gmm_v2` also declares VMEM scratch for partial output and zero fill. The 90% budget therefore admits the reported `tile_m=512` shape even though compilation exceeds the v4 core's 16 MiB VMEM. [tpu-inference #36](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/pull/36) fixes chip allocation, and [Marin #11781](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11781) pins that fix; neither changes this kernel. No result for the proposed v4-32/TP=16 run is posted here or in [#11855](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11855).

**Relevant code**

- [`gmm_v2.py#L962-L1041`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/03f10d39fd1786fdcd5cab1d1c98bc01c2b5155a/tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py#L962-L1041) — VMEM estimate and tile growth.
- [`gmm_v2.py#L1337-L1377`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/03f10d39fd1786fdcd5cab1d1c98bc01c2b5155a/tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py#L1337-L1377) — additional VMEM scratch.
- [`gmm_v2.py#L1307-L1308`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/03f10d39fd1786fdcd5cab1d1c98bc01c2b5155a/tpu_inference/kernels/megablox/gmm_v2.py#L1307-L1308) — 90% default budget.

# Proposed Fix

1. Complete the v4-32/TP=16 run with model revision `ac60d940`, the same backend pin and 32K context. Record the job, precompile outcome, a successful request, KV capacity, and latency. This establishes whether the 16-chip endpoint is usable.
2. If that run meets the endpoint's needs and its 16-chip footprint is acceptable, record the decision and close this issue as a v4-16 limitation.
3. If v4-16 is required, reproduce the failing shape in the tpu-inference fork and change tiling to account for the omitted scratch or reserve enough measured headroom. Add a regression for the selected v4 tile, verify full precompile and requests on v4-16, run the TPU release gate, then re-pin Marin in a PR with `Fixes #11920`.

spillover_issues.author: ClassicLarry
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is a human-guided, agent-executed experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

**Start with the [contributor guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_recipe/experiments/belay/CONTRIBUTING.md)**: how to check an idea against the recipe, pick a Track, follow its runs, and take it up the ladder.

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. One idea is one change judged against one control; several values of one setting (up to 4) count as one. Post combinations of changes as separate ideas, and a follow-up step (such as tuning the winner) as a new comment once the first result is in. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Plans, results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**The usual path for an idea:** optionally a `vanilla-*` Track first, for a radical idea or a stronger signal; then `speedrun`, for fast iteration and to check it fits the current recipe; then `hero-mfu` if it will change MFU a lot; then `ladder`. Maintainers promote ideas into the recipe from those results.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once, at the baseline's step count. After a `hero-mfu` result, each rung's steps are adjusted for the MFU change (better MFU, more steps). Without one, the verdict is provisional: the idea needs a `hero-mfu` result before it joins the recipe | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer runs it | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **[Admin](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#admin)** (maintainers, signed in to Marina): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

Notice: The majority of our compute right now is dedicated to SFT and RL runs. As a result, runs outside the speedrun track may queue up for a couple days.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try adding **spelling-normalised byte embeddings** to the input. Each token's input embedding row gets a learned sum over the first 8 UTF-8 bytes of its surface string, one 256 x d table per byte position. Read the bytes after stripping leading spaces and lowercasing, so " The", "the" and "The" share every byte row. Add two small feature rows to keep what the normalisation removes: leading space (0/1) and case (lower, capitalised, all caps, mixed). Zero-init the tables so the model starts identical to the baseline. Add the byte sum to the vocab table before the token gather, so there is no per-token cost and no extra communication. Input side only: do not share byte rows on the lm_head. Keep 8 byte positions and table width d_model at every rung.

Rationale: tokens that are spelling or case variants of each other start with unrelated embeddings and have to learn their similarity from context. Sharing byte rows gives the model that information directly, and it is information the body cannot compute from token ids. This is close to Spelling Bee Embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18030); the space/case normalisation is the addition.

comments.author: xTimeCrystal
comments.body: Track: speedrun Similar to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08888, try implementing a Full Bandwidth Transformer (FBT): the trunk runs K parallel passes over the sequence, and pass p's input at token t is fused from that token's embedding and the previous pass's output at token t-1: `x^{(p)}_{t} = norm(x_t + W_fuse norm(h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}))` - Use this formula, not the paper's. This is more stable. - `x_t` is the pass-1 input of token t (its embedding). - `h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}` is the final layer's output of pass `p-1` at position `t-1` (what the LM head reads), not that pass's input. - `norm` is parameter-free RMSNorm. - `W_fuse` is a `d_model` x `d_model` matrix, zero-initialised, so training starts as the plain model. - Position 0 and every document start (BOS) get the plain input `x_t`: no feedback across documents. - Gradients flow through all passes; do not detach or no-grad any pass. - Do not add "jitter" unlike the original paper - Training loss: CE of pass 1 + mean CE of the later passes (ignore as we only test K=2 passes). Evaluation: the last pass only. Sweep the fraction of training steps that use K=2 passes, the rest using K=1: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 (always 2 passes). Never use K=3. Evaluate every run with K=2. Optimise W_fuse with Muon first, at the learning rate and schedule of the other weight matrices. Then sweep 0.7x and 1.4x to bracket the optimal W_fuse lr using Muon. Then repeat the best Muon run with Adam on `W_fuse` (no weight decay), sweeping its learning rate over 0.7x, 1x, 1.4x. With MoE: keep the expert selections different across passes (the router picks again in every pass; never reuse pass 1's experts—we want the model's second pass picks to be adapted to the "enriched" hidden states). Quantile balancing counts the routing margins of all passes of a batch and updates the bias once, after the batch, for the next batch, never per pass: a per-pass update routes pass 2 with a bias computed from the same batch's own tokens, including later positions, which breaks causality. Compare against the dense baseline at matched training FLOPs: K=2 costs about 2x the FLOPs per token. Also, confirm that sequential decoding (token by token, each token fused with the previous token's final state) gives the same hidden-state and loss (within noise) as K=2 parallel passes. In our nanochat run they agreed to within 0.0003 bpb. nanochat results (per-iteration val bpb using the last pass; fbt2 = always 2 passes): This image shows the untuned baseline; it does not quite break even for the extra compute, and more tuning could close that gap.

Exact-match pointer mixture on the output with 8 candidates. For every position t, collect K = 8 candidate next tokens from earlier in the same document: for n = 1 and n = 2, the tokens that followed the 4 most recent earlier positions s < t whose last n tokens equal the n tokens ending at t (candidate x[s+1]). Mix them into the output: p(y) = (1 - G) p_vocab(y) + open * sum_k pi_k [c_k = y], where (pi_0, pi_1..pi_K) = softmax(0, l_1..l_K) over the candidates that exist, l_k = h . w_k + 8 * b[k, a_k] - 2 with h the lm_head input and a_k the number of other slots proposing the same token, G = open * sum_k pi_k, open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1). w [d_model, 8], b [8, 8] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M the pointer mass on the label. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Softcap radial MuonH: give each hidden matrix a learned, bounded radius on top of MuonH's sphere.

(Generated by an automated research harness. Edited to replace the earlier evidence with the completed results; bottom line first.)

**Bottom line**
- On Belay's 8-minute d512 speedrun, softcap beats the recipe's MuonH beyond the 0.005 band (below).
- That edge shrinks with size: on Belay's ladder recipe it is inside the band by d768 (one seed).
- Softcap does **not** beat a fairly tuned MuonW-family baseline. Once MuonW gets a tuned head LR and schedule-scaled decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), that baseline matches or beats softcap.
- So we are not proposing softcap as a ladder improvement on current evidence. d1024/d1280 are still running.

**Update rule (per Muon-group matrix slice W)**
- Write W = r0 · exp(s) · Ŵ, where r0 is the init radius and Ŵ is on the unit Frobenius sphere. Ŵ takes the usual MuonH hyperball step.
- s (a scalar log-radius per slice) is stepped by Adam on the radial gradient g = <∂L/∂W, W>, at the same LR and schedule as the matrix LR.
- Bound: outward steps are scaled by (1 − (s/c)²) and inward steps are taken in full. With c = 2 the radius is capped at e² ≈ 7.4× init.
- Slices whose output passes through a scale-removing norm keep a fixed radius (plain MuonH). Head and fallback groups are unchanged.

**d512 speedrun (Belay recipe, same-commit MuonH control)**
- Equal data, six paired GB200 seeds: softcap − MuonH mean −0.0083, one-sided 95% upper bound −0.0059, 6/6 seeds better. Three H100 seeds agree (mean −0.0082).
- An equal-time check gave smaller margins on the seeds read (about −0.004).
- learnable_qk_mult adds nothing (control + lqk +0.0002). The radius gain does transfer under the recipe's MLA q/k norms.

**Ladder (Belay recipe, one seed per rung; single-run gaps under 0.005 are ties)**
- Against MuonH: d512 −0.0103 (seed 1; −0.0057 on seed 0), d768 −0.0030 (a tie).
- Against the best MuonW-family run (MuonC, head LR ×0.35): d512 tie (−0.0025 on averaged reruns), d768 −0.0049 (a tie at the band edge).
- Same-seed reruns of identical settings at d512 differ by up to about 0.003, so one-seed margins below the band carry little weight.

**KMA d768 target (where the method was developed)**
- Softcap leads MuonW tuned on LR and decays by −0.0044 (seeds 2-11, held-out agreeing).
- That MuonW was under-tuned:
  - With MuonW's AdamW head LR tuned as well (×0.25-0.5), the lead drops to about −0.002, inside noise.
  - MuonC with a tuned head (2.4944, seed 0) beats every weight-normalized variant we tried, including softcap's best (2.5013).

**What we learned**
- Weight-normalized radial MuonH's apparent edge over MuonW came mostly from two things a fair MuonW also gets:
  - the AdamW head LR being too large;
  - plain decoupled decay shrinking the matrices late.
- MuonC's scheduled decay fixes the second, which matches the paper's prediction (flat late weight norm, bounded grad/weight ratio).

Document n-gram count cache mixed into the output. For each position t with label y, count over earlier positions s < t of the same packed document: c1 = number of s with x_s = x_t, n1 = number of those with x_{s+1} = y, c2 = number of s with (x_{s-1}, x_s) = (x_{t-1}, x_t) and n2 = number of those with x_{s+1} = y. Let q1 = n1 / c1 and q2 = n2 / c2 (each is a distribution over the vocabulary). Gate logits l_n = h . w_n + 8 * b_n * log2(1 + c_n) / 12 - 2 for n = 1, 2, where h is the lm_head input; (pi_0, pi_1, pi_2) = softmax(0, l_1, l_2) over the orders with c_n > 0; open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1); G = open * (pi_1 + pi_2). The model's distribution is p(y) = (1 - G) * p_vocab(y) + open * (pi_1 * q1(y) + pi_2 * q2(y)). w [d_model, 2], b [2] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M * exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M = open * (pi_1 * q1(label) + pi_2 * q2(label)). Implementation: all counts are integer work on the token ids, once per step before the forward pass and outside value_and_grad and any jax.checkpoint region. Per sequence, sort three key arrays stably with the position as payload: the token x_u; the pair id x_{u-1} * vocab + x_u; and the triple as two int32 keys (pair id of (x_{u-2}, x_{u-1}), x_u). A pair or triple that would cross a document start gets a key no other position has. In each sorted array a run breaks where the key or the document id changes; an element's rank is its index minus its run start (a cumulative max); scatter the ranks back to positions. Then c1(t) = rank_token[t], c2(t) = rank_pair[t], n1(t) = rank_pair[t + 1] and n2(t) = rank_triple[t + 1]. Take ce from the existing fused cross-entropy kernel with per-token reduction; no second pass over the vocabulary, no [batch, seq, vocab] tensor, no lm_head row gather. Target step time within 1% of the control. Same settings at every rung.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

At each step of training, we estimate the gradient against the 'weights', where the weights is a weighted sum over all prior gradients. However this weighted sum has a restricted set of options because we only modify it via new_update + modifier*all_prior_updates. A richer set is possible. Try this:

Implement linear init removal in our Hyperball optimizer. For every weight matrix Hyperball constrains (attention and MLP matrices; leave embeddings and norm gains alone), keep a scalar b, the coefficient of the initial weights W₀ in the current weights. It starts at 1.0. Regenerate W₀ from the init seed rather than storing a copy. On every step, keep b updated as b ← a·b, where a = R/‖W − ηV‖ is Hyperball’s projection factor. From step N/3 to step 2N/3, subtract a fixed amount of the init before projecting: W ← W − ηV − d·W₀ with d = min(δ, b), then project back to radius R, and update b ← a·(b − d). Pick δ so b reaches exactly 0 at step 2N/3. A good start is δ ≈ b(N/3) divided by the number of steps in the window, then adjust slightly to account for the shrinking from projection. Outside that window the optimizer is unchanged.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**Learned-radius MuonH (nonsi) plus an s(t)² head and late-matrix anneal.** This changes only the optimizer. It adds one scalar per matrix slice and no model change.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule):
1. *Learned radius ("nonsi").* Write each MuonH-group slice as W = r0 · exp(ρ) · Ŵ, with r0 = ‖W‖_F at init and Ŵ on the unit sphere.
   - Ŵ takes MuonH's hyperball step, unchanged.
   - ρ (one scalar per slice) is stepped by Adam (β 0.9 / 0.99) on the radial gradient ⟨∂L/∂W, W⟩, at the matrix LR and its usual (unannealed) schedule. There is no cap.
   - Slices whose output feeds a norm through linear maps only (so ⟨∂L/∂W, W⟩ = 0) keep ρ = 0, i.e. plain MuonH. These are the MLA kv down-projection (w_dkv), the MLA query (w_q) and key up-projection (w_uk), and the MoE latent down-projection (w_latent_down). The KDA write-strength group learns ρ at its own LR.
2. *Head anneal.* The lm_head / output_proj (AdamH) LR becomes lr_max · s(t)² instead of lr_max · s(t).
3. *Late matrix anneal.* From step t₀ = round(0.7937 · N), multiply the MuonH matrix LR by s(t) / s(t₀), so the angular step falls as s(t)² from there and is continuous at t₀.

The Adam groups are unchanged. With ρ ≡ 0 and both anneals off, this is the recipe.

**Evidence** (our own runs, Paloma macro loss)

*8-minute d512 speedrun, equal data, 6 paired seeds, against a same-commit recipe MuonH control (mean 3.0423):*

| Arm | Δ vs MuonH |
|---|---|
| nonsi + s² anneals (this) | **−0.0115** (all 6 seeds; one-sided 95% bound −0.0098) |
| nonsi without the anneals | −0.0079 |
| MuonC (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), λ 0.1, + the same anneals | −0.0033 |
| MuonC, λ 0.2, + the same anneals | −0.0161 |

*d512 on the ladder recipe (10,767 steps), seed 1:* this 2.8518; recipe MuonH 2.8697 (+0.018); nonsi without the anneals 2.8604 (+0.009).

**Caveats**
- A tuned MuonC with the same anneals beats this on the speedrun: at λ 0.2 it is 0.0046 better (five of six seeds). The anneals are not specific to the learned radius.
- On the larger ladder rungs, the same anneals helped our capped variant (softcap) less and less: −0.008 at d512, −0.010 at d768, −0.004 at d1024, and +0.006 (worse) at d1280. nonsi with the anneals at d768 to d1280 is still running.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**MuonC with an s(t)² head and late-matrix anneal.** This replaces MuonH's sphere with Muon plus schedule-scaled weight decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), and adds the two anneals from our nonsi intake above. It changes only the optimizer, with no new parameters.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps):
1. *Matrix LR with a late anneal.* lr_m(t) = lr_t until t₀ = round(0.7937 · N), then lr_m(t) = lr_t · s(t) / s(t₀). The angular step falls as s(t)² from t₀ and is continuous there.
2. *MuonC matrices.* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrix takes W ← W − lr_m(t) · (O + λ_t W), with no projection to a sphere.
   - O is the Muon direction MuonH already computes: Newton–Schulz with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - λ_t = λ · lr_m(t) / lr_max, with λ = 0.2.
   - KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR multiple.
3. *Head.* lm_head / output_proj use AdamW instead of AdamH, at LR lr_max · s(t)², with decoupled decay 0.05.
4. *Adam groups.* They keep their recipe LRs, with AdamW decay 0.05 on rank ≥ 2 leaves, replacing the recipe's annealed gate/router decay.

This differs from X0243/X0244 in the two anneals, the AdamW head, and the decay schedule λ · lr_t / lr_max. Both parts matter on the speedrun. At λ 0.1 the anneals are worth 0.006, and raising λ to 0.2 adds another 0.013.

**Evidence** (our own runs, Paloma macro loss)

*8-minute d512 speedrun, equal data, 6 paired seeds, against a same-commit recipe MuonH control (mean 3.0423):*

| Arm | Δ vs MuonH |
|---|---|
| MuonC λ 0.2 + anneals (this) | **−0.0161** (better on all 6 seeds, −0.011 to −0.020) |
| MuonC λ 0.4 + anneals | −0.0135 |
| MuonC λ 0.1 + anneals | −0.0033 |
| MuonC λ 0.1, no anneals | +0.0025 |
| nonsi + the same anneals (our other intake) | −0.0115 |

λ was picked on these seeds from a grid of λ (0.025 to 0.4) and LR multiplier (0.5× to 1.41×). λ 0.2 and 0.4 are close, and both beat λ 0.1 by far more than picking the best grid cell would add by chance. Every LR change was worse. λ 0.8 is still running.

*Belay ladder recipe, seed 1, λ 0.1 (not yet tuned on the ladder) + anneals vs recipe MuonH:*

| Rung | d512 | d768 | d1024 | d1280 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Δ | −0.013 | −0.009 | −0.010 | −0.010 |

This was the best run on every rung we measured. A λ sweep on the ladder (0.2 to 0.4 at d512 and d768) is starting.

**Caveats**
- The ladder numbers are one seed per rung, with seed-to-seed spread of about 0.003–0.006 in paired gaps.
- Equal-time numbers are not in yet. The matrix step costs the same as MuonH's, apart from skipping the sphere projection.

Given the speedrun win of X0250 (Muon with matrix decay lambda 0.2, late matrix anneal, AdamC head, router and embed), run its 4 rung scaling ladder.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: ladder

**Law-cap ball: MuonH's matrices take a plain Muon step inside a per-layer Frobenius ball whose radius comes from a closed-form law, plus the s(t)² head anneal and late matrix anneal from our earlier intakes.** There is no weight decay and nothing to tune per rung. The change is optimizer-only, with no new parameters.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps)
1. *Matrices.* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength slice W takes W′ = W − η_t U. If ‖W′‖_F exceeds cap_l, W′ is rescaled onto the ball; otherwise it is kept as is. There is no decay and no projection inside the ball.
   - U is the Muon direction MuonH already computes: Newton–Schulz with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - η_t is the recipe's MuonH LR. From t₀ = round(0.7937 · N) it is multiplied by s(t)/s(t₀) (late anneal). KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR.
   - A slice is a 2-D leaf, or one layer of a stacked leaf.
2. *Cap, from shape and peak LR only.*
   - cap_l = κ · |U_l|, where |U_l| = √(n · min(in, out) · max(1, out/in)) is the Frobenius norm of an orthogonalized update for that slice, and n is the number of matrices in the slice.
   - κ = √(τ · lr_max / (2λ)), with τ = 39 and λ = 0.2. This is the size MuonC's matrices settle at for decay λ (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285). The ball reaches it directly instead of decaying toward it.
3. *Head.* The recipe's AdamH head, with LR lr_max · s(t)² instead of lr_max · s(t).
4. *Adam groups.* Unchanged.

**Evidence** (our own runs on the Belay ladder recipe, seed 1, Paloma macro loss)

| Rung | this | recipe MuonH | Δ | MuonC (λ 0.1) + same anneals, same commit | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | 2.8538 | 2.8697 | −0.016 | 2.8569 | −0.003 |
| d768 | 2.6051 | 2.6148 | −0.010 | 2.6062 | −0.001 |
| d1024 | 2.4045 | 2.4075 | −0.003 | 2.3997 | +0.005 |
| d1280 | 2.2627 | 2.2749 | −0.012 | 2.2656 | −0.003 |

- The matrices sit on their caps from early in training. A checkpoint check confirmed this on every rung.
- The cap level is bracketed around the law. At d512, 0.5× and 1.4× the law's cap are clearly worse, and 0.7× ties. At d768, 0.7× is worse and 1.4× is within noise.
- On the 8-minute d512 speedrun (6 seeds) it ties tuned MuonC + the same anneals (+0.0004 vs λ 0.4).

**Caveats**
- One seed per rung. Seed-to-seed spread of paired gaps is about 0.003–0.006, and a second d1280 seed has been proposed.
- It ties, rather than beats, a tuned MuonC with the same anneals (our other intake). Its appeal is that it gets there with no decay to tune: the cap is set from shape and peak LR alone, and the same formula was used at every rung.
- It also avoids a failure we saw with a learned-radius variant (softcap + the same anneals), which fell 0.016 behind at d1280.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: ladder

X0250 4 rung scaling ladder with a per-rung matrix decay. This replaces our earlier X0250 ladder request (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-7029815277); please run this one instead of that one.

Keep X0250 exactly at every rung except the matrix decay lambda in lambda_t = lambda * lr_m(t) / lr_max. Instead of the constant 0.2, set lambda per rung so the total matrix decay over the run, lambda * lr_max * N, stays at its d512-rung value: lambda_rung = 0.2 * (lr_max_d512 * N_d512) / (lr_max_rung * N_rung), where lr_max is the rung's MuonH-group peak LR and N its number of steps. d512 keeps 0.2; larger rungs get smaller lambda. This holds the weights' decay timescale at a fixed fraction of training, and it matches the MuonC decay optima WhenWen measured on this ladder (0.2 at d512, about 0.1 at d768; #11785). Everything else is X0250's at every rung: the MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrices step W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with no sphere projection and the late matrix anneal from t0 = round(0.7937 * N); lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2 from that rung's head peak; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W from that rung's Adam peak; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No new parameters or state.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖

Track: custom

Rerun the recipe with no flag on competitive-d1024 and competitive-d1280 from this week's branch (seed 0, each Track's own command). Then judge finished ladders against the mean of that run and the s7n run at each rung.

Every competitive rung compares a variant with one finished run (`s7n-d1024`, `s7n-d1280L16`). `belay_s7.py` says the s7n runs were trained on `marin_belay_v1_fp8quality` at `a5a8647840`, which is not an ancestor of the weekly branches. The registry still labels these baselines "(same commit, seed 0)", from the template in `registry_entry.py` line 257.

To first order, `ladder_projection` gives Δ_hero = −0.533·Δd512 − 0.115·Δd768 + 0.434·Δd1024 + 0.980·Δd1280. This reproduces the six recorded projections. A baseline offset at d1280 therefore passes almost fully into every ladder's verdict.

In the six finished ladders (X0014, X0073, X0221, X0226, X0235, X0237), the mean Δ is −0.0134, −0.0093, −0.0079 and −0.0010 from d512 to d1280. From d1024 to d1280, Δ moves toward zero in all six (mean +0.0069); from d768 to d1024 it moves +0.0014. The seed-1 recipe runs in #11785 are +0.0016, +0.0027, −0.0031 and +0.0043 relative to s7n, with the same signs at d1024 and d1280. Measured against them, the d1280 drop disappears and every projection moves by −0.0017. #11785 also found that an apparent d512 lead of −0.0045 was cross-commit noise once rerun on the same commit; the s7n baselines are cross-commit by construction.

A d1280 rerun 0.003 or more above 2.2706 would mean that every ladder's d1280 Δ is biased toward a loss by that amount. A rerun within 0.001 of it rules this out. The d1280 rung also differs from d1024 in batch (1,024 sequences, the hero's tokens per step), steps (20,023 against 39,210) and depth (16 layers), so the rerun separates the baseline from those changes.

Budget: two runs, about 1,010 minutes on one node (d1024) and 1,003 minutes on four nodes (d1280), using the run times on the Belay page.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body: 🤖 Thanks for running X0254. The [report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_registry/experiments/belay/analysis/X0254/report.md) reads d1280 alone: 2.2716 against 2.2706 for `s7n-d1280L16`, +0.0010, inconclusive. The d1024 rerun finished at 2.4095 against 2.4106 for s7n, an offset of -0.0011 in the other direction. With both reruns as the baseline, the ladder rule's weights (+0.43 at d1024, +0.98 at d1280) move every projection by about -0.0005. None of the seven complete ladders (X0014, X0073, X0221, X0226, X0235, X0237, X0238) changes verdict, and each projection stays at least 0.0017 from the ±0.005 edges. So at these two rungs the s7n baseline from the other commit holds to about 0.001, and I see no need to rerun d512 and d768.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

**Try debiased sampled softmax so the d512 recipe can train on more tokens per GPU-second.** Compute a cheap vocabulary-shortlist loss at every training position, always including its target token. Split each sequence into blocks of 16 positions and sample one position per block. At that position compute the recipe’s full-vocabulary loss and add the difference from the shortlist loss, divided by the position’s sampling probability. Give every position positive probability, stop gradients through those probabilities, and apply the recipe’s token weights and normalization. In expectation this recovers the full training-loss gradient, including gradients to the output weights. Use exact full-vocabulary loss for Paloma evaluation.

The starting settings come from a frozen 4-layer, width-128 LM with a 128,256-token vocabulary. We used a 16,384-row shortlist and 64 full-vocabulary positions per 1,024-token sequence. On one GPU the native full-head batch of 8 took 53.8 ms. The corrected head at batch 128 took 44.1 ms and had 6.96% of that batch-8 gradient variance. Both batch size and head computation changed in this comparison. It motivates testing whether the throughput gain translates to lower validation loss on Belay. [Frozen-checkpoint measurements](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/gradient-variance-frontier/runs/8e66d762264394)

For Belay, start with a shortlist of roughly one eighth of its vocabulary and the same one-in-16 correction rate. Compare against the current fused head at equal training tokens first, then spend the measured throughput gain on more tokens in the 8-minute run. Report tokens/sec and full-vocabulary Paloma macro loss for both. Submitted with Codex assistance.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: ladder

Follow-up to X0250's per-rung matrix decay ladder: put the Adam-side decays on the same timescale rule. X0250's ladder holds lambda * lr_max * N fixed for the matrices, but its Adam-side decay coefficients are constants, so their total decay over the run (coefficient * adam_lr_max * N) grows about 2x from d512 to d1024, and token_embed ends progressively smaller relative to the baseline's at larger rungs.

Keep X0250's ladder exactly (the per-rung matrix lambda from lambda * lr_max * N held at its d512-rung value, the late matrix anneal, the s(t)^2 AdamC head with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2) and change two coefficients per rung. Let A = adam_lr_max * N, the Adam group's peak LR times the number of steps, and A_d512 its value at the d512 rung (about 33.5). (1) The MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * c * W, with c = 0.3 * A_d512 / A_rung instead of the constant 0.3. (2) The other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW with decoupled decay 0.05 * A_d512 / A_rung instead of the constant 0.05. That gives about 0.3 / 0.175 / 0.147 / 0.199 and 0.05 / 0.029 / 0.025 / 0.033 at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. The d512 rung is identical to X0250's d512 rung, so it can be reused. No new parameters or state.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the end of the late matrix anneal. X0250's matrix LR after t0 = round(0.7937 * N) is lr_m(t) = lr_t * s(t) / s(t0), with s(t) = lr_t / lr_max, so it ends at (min_lr_ratio^2 / s(t0)) * lr_max, a third or less of the schedule's own floor, and the matrices nearly stop training over the last few percent of the run. Clamp it from below at the schedule's floor: lr_m(t) = max(lr_t * s(t) / s(t0), min_lr_ratio * lr_max). The matrix decay keeps lambda_t = lambda * lr_m(t) / lr_max with lambda = 0.2, so it follows the clamped LR. Everything else is X0250's: the MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrices step W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with no sphere projection; lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No new parameters or state. Target step time equal to X0250.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Compare the benefits of different activation control methods for the lm_head part, whether these benefits are repetitive or complementary, then decide which combination to use.
There are binary design choices for each of them:
A. vanilla rmsnorm vs gatednorm, before applying lm_head
B. raw results vs tanh capped results, after applying lm_head
C. without z-loss vs with z-loss, for the lm_head outputs
So there are 2^3=8 possibilities in the whole design space.

Rationale: There are inconsistent results on whether gatednorm-for-lm-head/tanh cap/z-loss-for-lm-head is beneficial at all, across the arch hill climbing history, and I suspect it's because sometimes one of the features here is used with the other, and sometimes it is not. So I suggest that it's time we figure this out with more clarity.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**Law-cap ball (X0253) for the matrices, with X0250's AdamC head and Adam-side decays.** This is optimizer-only. The head stores one scalar per slice, and nothing else is added.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps, t₀ = round(0.7937 · N))
1. *Matrices (X0253).* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength slice takes W′ = W − η_t U. If ‖W′‖_F > cap_l, W′ is rescaled onto the ball; otherwise it is kept as is. There is no decay and no projection inside the ball.
   - U is MuonH's Newton–Schulz direction, with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - η_t is the recipe's MuonH LR. From t₀ it is multiplied by s(t) / s(t₀). KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR.
   - cap_l = κ · √(n · min(in, out) · max(1, out/in)), with κ = √(39 · lr_max / (2 · 0.2)) and lr_max the rung's own MuonH peak. The same formula applies at every rung; nothing is tuned per rung.
2. *Head (X0250).* lm_head / output_proj use AdamC instead of AdamH. For each slice, store r0 = ‖W‖_F at init, take U = the Adam direction normalized per slice, and update W ← W − lr_h(t) · r0 · U − (lr_h(t)² / lr_hmax) · λ_h · W, with no projection. Here lr_h(t) = lr_hmax · s(t)² and λ_h = 25 · lr_hmax / 2.
3. *Router and token embedding (X0250).* The MoE router matrices (not the router bias, not attn_gate) and token_embed keep Adam's update, with decay (adam_lr_t² / adam_lr_max) · 0.3 · W. This replaces the annealed router decay.
4. *Other Adam leaves (X0250).* Rank ≥ 2 leaves get AdamW decay 0.05.

Compared with X0250, only step 1 changes: the ball replaces the schedule-scaled matrix decay. Compared with X0253, only steps 2–4 change.

**Why**
- *Ladder, same control and seed 0.* X0250 is −0.0178 / −0.0130 at d512 / d768. X0253 is −0.0077 / −0.0106 / −0.0092 / −0.0073 at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280.
- *Our own runs.* The ball ties MuonC with the same two anneals on every rung (−0.003 to +0.005, seed 1) and on the speedrun (6 seeds). So X0250's extra lead over X0253 likely comes from its head and Adam-side decays, which X0253 did not have. On the speedrun, X0250 (AdamC head) beats X0247 (the same matrices with an AdamW head) by 0.006.
- *No per-rung matrix decay.* The cap comes from shape and peak LR alone, so the matrices need no λ and no per-rung λ rule.

**Prediction:** on the speedrun, within ±0.005 of X0250 (−0.0203). If it ties there, the ladder is the real test: X0250 needs its per-rung λ rule at d1024 / d1280, and this does not.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the schedule of the matrix decay coefficient. X0250 uses lambda_t = lambda * lr_m(t) / lr_max (lambda = 0.2), which holds the matrices' equilibrium norm fixed when the norm growth per step scales as lr_m(t)^2, the case for momentum-correlated gradient noise. Measured on X0250's own norm logs, the growth per unit lr_m(t)^2 is not constant: it rises as the LR falls (attention matrices about 17 at 80% of peak LR, 21 at 19%, 40 at 3%; routed experts 34, 45, 102). The ladder runs show the same rise at every rung. That fits an added term in the growth that is first order in the LR, lr_m(t) * lr_max * K, next to the second-order term lr_m(t)^2 * D. Balancing decay against both terms gives lambda_t = lambda * ((1 - f) * lr_m(t) / lr_max + f) with f = K / (D + K); the fits give f of about 0.04 to 0.10 across the matrix groups. Use f = 0.05 and lambda = 0.2 for every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrix: each still steps W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with no sphere projection, KDA write strength at its 2x LR with the same lambda_t. lr_m(t) is X0250's matrix LR including the late matrix anneal from t0 = round(0.7937 * N). Relative to X0250 the decay coefficient is 1.05x at peak LR, about 1.2x at t0 and about 4x on the last step. Everything else is X0250's: lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No new parameters or state. Target step time equal to X0250.

comments.author: ykyaol7
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Revisit the potential of looped transformers. Unlike X0036, try middle-loop transformers with two attention residual designs, inspired by Inkling-mini https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05234.

Use 2 prelude layers + 2 shared middle layers + 2 coda layers, testing 2 and 3 middle passes. Use one AttnRes block per Transformer layer and restart each pass from the prelude state, accessing previous-pass information through AttnRes. Share middle-layer weights and AttnRes queries across passes. No need to add explicit embedding injection at loop boundaries: both designs already retain the embedding as an AttnRes source.

1. Inkling-style local + cross-loop AttnRes: local AttnRes reads embedding, prelude blocks, and available current-pass blocks; separate cross-loop AttnRes reads the previous pass’s two middle blocks. Combine their outputs u, m using z = W_down [RMSNorm(u); RMSNorm(m)], f = tanh(W_f z), g = tanh(W_g z), and h = (1 − f) * u + g * m, where * is elementwise multiplication and the bottleneck rank is 64. Controllers are separate per attention/MLP sublayer but shared across passes; initialize W_f and W_g to zero. Use one combined input for Q/K/V. The first pass uses only local AttnRes.

2. Sliding-window depth AttnRes: at every middle attention/MLP sublayer, use a single AttnRes pool that always includes the embedding and all prelude blocks, plus the immediately previous loop’s two middle blocks (if any) and the current loop’s available blocks.

For both designs, coda reads the embedding, all prelude blocks, only the final pass’s middle blocks, and its own available blocks.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the direction of the lm_head (output_proj, shape [d, V]) update. X0250's head is AdamC: Adam's per-element direction, normalized over the whole matrix, stepped at lr_h(t) * r0 with decay (lr_h(t)^2 / lr_hmax) * lambda_h * W. Each token's column of output_proj sets that token's logit, so its column norm is that token's logit scale; per-element Adam normalization mixes those scales across tokens. Replace the direction with a per-token normalized momentum direction (the row-norm update for vocabulary-indexed matrices; Lau & Su, arXiv 2605.18106; MuonIO, arXiv 2610.02705): keep a momentum buffer M <- 0.95 M + 0.05 G and take the Nesterov input N = 0.05 G + 0.95 M; subtract the mean over the vocab axis (the component that shifts every logit equally), divide each token column N[:, v] by its L2 norm (eps 1e-8), and subtract the vocab mean again to get U. Step W <- W - lr_h(t) * 0.02 * sqrt(d) * U - (lr_h(t)^2 / lr_hmax) * lambda_h * W, so the whole-matrix step norm equals X0250's lr_h(t) * r0 at init (within 1.3%). Keep X0250's head LR (the s(t)^2 head schedule), lr_hmax and lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2, and its gradient clipping; no sphere projection. Everything else is X0250's: the MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrices step W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with lambda_t = 0.2 * lr_m(t) / lr_max, no sphere projection, and the late matrix anneal from t0 = round(0.7937 * N); the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. Optimizer state: one fp32 momentum buffer for the head in place of Adam's two moments. Target step time equal to X0250.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the size the matrices settle at, while holding their rotation per step fixed. Under X0250's rule the MuonH-group matrices step W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with lambda_t = lambda * lr_m(t) / lr_max, so the shrink per step is lambda * lr_m(t)^2 / lr_max. Balancing that against the norm growth from the orthogonalized updates gives an equilibrium norm with norm^2 proportional to lr_max / lambda and an angle turned per step proportional to sqrt(lambda * lr_max) * lr_m(t) / lr_max. Raising lr_max by sqrt(2) and dividing lambda by sqrt(2) therefore keeps the angle per step and the shrink per step exactly as in X0250 at every step, and only makes every matrix settle at sqrt(2) times X0250's norm. Change: matrix peak LR lr_max -> sqrt(2) * lr_max (the whole matrix schedule lr_m(t) scales by sqrt(2), including warmup and the late matrix anneal from t0 = round(0.7937 * N)), and lambda 0.2 -> 0.141421, with lambda_t = 0.141421 * lr_m(t) / lr_max computed from the new lr_max. KDA write strength keeps its 2x LR multiple of the new matrix LR and the same lambda_t. Every other learning rate keeps its absolute X0250 value: if the head, router, embedding or other Adam LRs are defined as multiples of the matrix LR, divide those multiples by sqrt(2) so their values do not change. Everything else is X0250's: lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No sphere projection, no new parameters or state. Target step time equal to X0250.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the starting norm of the matrices X0250's MuonC decay acts on. Under X0250's rule (W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W), lambda_t = 0.2 * lr_m(t) / lr_max) each matrix grows from its init norm to an equilibrium norm about 1.6 to 2.7 times its init (attention about 1.6, shared expert about 1.7 to 2.0, routed experts and the latent projections about 2.0 to 2.7) and reaches it within the first 5 to 10% of training; until then its angle turned per step is larger than at equilibrium, because the same update lands on a smaller matrix. Start at equilibrium instead: after the model's normal initialization and before the first step, multiply the initial value of every matrix that X0250 steps with the MuonC rule (the MuonH group: attention projections, MoE routed, shared and latent matrices, the GatedNorm matrices; and the KDA write-strength matrices) by 2.0. Every other parameter (token_embed, lm_head / output_proj, MoE router weights, gains, biases, 1-D parameters) keeps its normal init, with the same seed. Training is otherwise X0250's: the same matrix schedule with its late matrix anneal from t0 = round(0.7937 * N) and lambda_t as above, no sphere projection; lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No new parameters or state. Target step time equal to X0250.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the token_embed update. Each embedding row is read through an RMSNorm, so the forward pass depends only on each row's direction; under X0250's Adam update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W the row lengths serve only to set, indirectly, how far each row turns per step. Set that turn directly with a per-row hyperball step and drop the decay. Keep a momentum buffer M <- 0.95 M + 0.05 G for token_embed (shape [V, d]) and take the Nesterov input N = 0.05 G + 0.95 M. For each row i: u_i = N_i / (||N_i|| + 1e-8); then W_i <- r_i * normalize(W_i - theta_t * r_i * u_i), where r_i is row i's L2 norm at initialization (held fixed for the whole run) and normalize(x) = x / ||x||. The turn per step is theta_t = 0.012 * adam_lr_t / adam_lr_max, with X0250's Adam LR schedule (warmup and cosine), so the step angle at peak is about X0250's measured per-row turn per step. No weight decay on token_embed. Optimizer state: one fp32 momentum buffer for token_embed in place of Adam's two moments. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen (drafted by a Claude Code session).

Track: speedrun

**ID Balancing in place of QB for the router bias** ([arXiv 2609.39137](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39137), Jin et al., Qwen). This changes only the per-step update of `router_bias`. Routing (top-K on biased logits, stop-gradient bias), combine weights and all parameters stay the same.

**What changes.** Today each step sets `router_bias = −β`, where β is the per-expert (1−K/E) quantile of the previous step's logit margins (Kimi QB). In the paper's PID view this is a pure proportional controller: it tracks each batch's target and keeps no memory of past load errors. ID Balancing instead accumulates the load error. Per MoE layer and per step, it uses the global token counts n_i that `routing_counts_per_layer` already reduces:

1. n̄ = mean_i n_i, e_i = (n̄ − n_i) / n̄
2. Δe_i = e_i − e_i^prev, g_i = 1[e_i^prev · Δe_i > 0]. The gate is open only while an imbalance grows without crossing zero, and it is closed at step 0.
3. b_i ← b_i + K_i·e_i + K_d·g_i·Δe_i, then b ← b − mean(b), then e^prev ← e. b starts at 0.

The bias is applied with the same one-step lag as `pending_qb_betas`. b and e^prev are training state, so they go in the checkpoint. The QB histogram becomes unused, which saves one bincount and psum per layer.

**Gains (one setting, 3 values).** The paper uses K_i = K_d = 6e-3, with the bias added to sigmoid scores σ(z). The recipe adds the bias to logits instead. At the selection cutoff Δz ≈ Δs / σ′(z*), and σ′ ≤ 1/4, so in logit units the paper's gain is at least 4× larger. Sweep K_i = K_d ∈ {6e-3, 2.4e-2, 9.6e-2}: the paper's value, ×4 and ×16. Because e is normalized by n̄, the gains have no dependence on width or E, so every rung would use the same gains.

**Why it might help here**
- The EP capacity factor is 1.05, so tokens above 1.05·n̄ on an expert are dropped (`capacity_overflow`). Lower peak overload means fewer dropped tokens. In the paper's 18.9B / 120B-token runs (768 experts), ID beat QB on worst backbone MaxVio: 15.3 vs 31.1 at top-3, 10.3 vs 21.2 at top-5 and 8.4 vs 10.1 at top-10. It also beat QB on last-1k MinVio at every K (0.53 vs 0.65 at top-3).
- The derivative term's gains come in the first ~5k steps, and the speedrun is 2,817 steps.
- Earlier Belay tries at giving the QB bias memory lost at d512: X0158 (damped QB, γ 0.5 / 0.3) was +0.0007 / +0.0017, and X0029 (QB frozen at mid-run) was +0.0069. Those smoothed or froze a proportional target. The paper's EMA-on-QB diagnostic reproduces that trade-off, since smoothing slows correction. ID gets memory by integrating count errors instead, and the paper reports that this keeps correction fast while cutting late bias drift.

**Caveats**
- The paper's LM-loss gaps among the bias-based methods are small. ID vs QB is −0.0006 / −0.0004 / −0.0015 at top-3 / 5 / 10, inside the 0.005 band. A win here would come mostly from fewer dropped tokens. Please log `capacity_overflow` and per-layer MaxVio / MinVio next to Paloma.
- The recipe's routing (8 of 384, K/E = 1/48) is less sparse than the paper's 1/77 to 1/256, and the paper says ID's advantage grows with sparsity.
- Average backbone MaxVio was slightly lower for QB at top-5 and top-10 (0.64 vs 0.65, 0.48 vs 0.51). ID won on worst-case and on underload, not on every metric.
