spillover_issues.author: lukedhlee
spillover_issues.body:
**TL;DR**

- I checked every r2egym task in TaskTrove v4.12 the simplest way: run it with no fix (the tests should fail) and run it with the gold patch (the tests should pass). No model involved. 2,614 of the 3,035 active tasks behave correctly.
- The 421 pandas and numpy tasks give reward 1 no matter what the agent does. The verifier tests the pandas or numpy release pre-installed in the image, which already contains the fix, and never imports the agent's checkout under `/testbed`. Constant reward, so no training signal.
- The oracle-only selection kept exactly those tasks, because for these repos "gold patch passes" and "no fix passes" are the same condition. About 1,700 pandas and numpy tasks that would have been fine were dropped instead.
- Separately, 25 tasks have a gold patch that fails its own tests (finding 3).
- Task lists, gate reports, and 2,748 additional gated R2E-Gym tasks are linked below.

**Scope.** Source subdirectory `laion__r2egym-patched-full-oracle-v3` in TaskTrove v4.12, 3,035 active tasks. I ran the check in two setups: R2E-Gym's original per-task images under Apptainer (all tasks), and TaskTrove's own flattened images under Daytona (2,476 tasks). What differs between them is the image, not the sandbox; the no-op pass reproduces on Daytona and in a plain local Python env alike, and does not happen on the per-task images. Per-repo census: [link](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f0a696a7-a69c-42d6-badb-a93a477bfff8).

## Findings

**1. All 421 active pandas and numpy tasks pass their hidden tests with no fix.** Their setup skips the editable install because the source will not build on those old commits, so the tests run against the pandas or numpy wheel baked into the image, not the checkout. A wheel cannot see edits under `/testbed`, so any patch or none passes. On TaskTrove's flattened images (Daytona): pandas 268/268 and numpy 144/144 passed with both no fix and the gold patch. On R2E-Gym's per-task images (Apptainer) the same tasks behave correctly, so the tasks themselves are sound.

The oracle-only selection appears to be what kept them. For these two repos the gold patch passes exactly when the wheel already behaves the way the expected output wants, which is the same condition under which no fix passes. The filter therefore selected the non-discriminative tasks and dropped the roughly 1,700 pandas and numpy tasks that would have been fine.

**2. On TaskTrove's flattened images (Daytona), the same no-op pass hits scattered tasks in other repos.** Pillow 25 of 574, orange3 10 of 48, coveragepy 3, datalad 2, sympy 1. These repos do try to install the checkout, but their setup ends in `pip install -e . || pip install . || true`, so if that install fails it is ignored and the tests fall back to whichever version was already in the image, giving the same no-op pass.

**3. On R2E-Gym's per-task images (Apptainer), the gold patch fails its own tests on 25 tasks** (tornado 8, numpy 8, datalad 6, orange3 2, pandas 1). The oracle solution scores 0, so these tasks can never reach reward 1 and are unusable for a different reason than finding 1. One more sympy task times out before its verifier returns. This looks like an upstream R2E-Gym issue rather than a TaskTrove one; exclusion is probably enough. Full list in `gold_patch_fails_on_r2egym_images.tsv`.

**4. Provenance.** v3.20 rewrote `base_commit` and `test_info.json:docker_image` to the parent commit, so joining back to R2E-Gym-V1 on those fields maps 391 rows to the wrong image. Joining on the hidden test files works ([mapping](https://github.com/lukedhlee/OpenThoughts-Agent/blob/904bb6c4f66efc10cc6bbab4b8e75261d63eb148/data/r2egym/overlap/tasktrove_v3_upstream_map.tsv)).

The 293 text-less matplotlib and moto tasks that v4.12 dropped come from upstream, where every row of those two repos has an empty `problem_statement`. Nothing more to do there.

## Task lists

All in [one folder](https://github.com/lukedhlee/OpenThoughts-Agent/tree/904bb6c4f66efc10cc6bbab4b8e75261d63eb148/data/r2egym/overlap/tasktrove_v3_gate) as TSV, each row with the upstream R2E-Gym-V1 image for the task:

- `wheel_only_pandas_numpy_active.tsv`, the 421 active pandas and numpy tasks
- `daytona_pass_with_no_fix.tsv`, the 453 tasks whose pristine run scored 1 on TaskTrove's images
- `gold_patch_fails_on_r2egym_images.tsv`, the 25 oracle failures plus one verifier timeout
- `empty_issue_text_removed_in_v4.12.tsv`, the 293 text-less tasks
- the two gate reports and the paired pass@8 comparison

## Suggestions

- Repackage or drop the 421 pandas and numpy tasks in TaskTrove's flattened form. The tasks themselves are fine and run correctly on R2E-Gym's per-task images, where the commit is compiled in; only TaskTrove's flattened packaging of them is broken. To keep the flattened form, the tests need to import the checked-out commit: compile the commit into the image (one image per task, as upstream R2E-Gym does) or restore a cache of the compiled files per commit. Until one of those is in place, drop them from the active set so nothing trains on a no-op reward.
- Add a one-line check to the verifier: `python -c "import pandas; assert pandas.__file__.startswith('/testbed')"`. It fails the task whenever the tests would run against the wrong package, which also catches the sporadic cases in finding 2.
- Run every task once with no fix and require the tests to fail, alongside the existing gold-patch check. Checking only that the gold patch passes cannot see this class of bug.
- 2,748 more R2E-Gym-V1 tasks pass the same check on per-task images and are not in TaskTrove (pandas 1,167, numpy 601, orange3 429, aiohttp 195, and the rest, listed in `raw_set_gated_not_in_tasktrove.tsv`). With the fix above that roughly doubles the clean r2egym set. They only work on per-task images or with the compiled-files cache, so adding them depends on how firm the snapshot budget is. I can build the repaired v4 parquet in the current TaskTrove layout.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
Builds of the patched PJRT wheel in `marin-community/xla` cache `~/.cache/bazel` wholesale, about 11.6 GB against GitHub's documented 10 GB per-repository limit. Retention is unpredictable, and the difference is 1m35s of build time versus 3h31m.

| run | restore | build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [33013385685](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33013385685) | 3m38s | 1m35s |
| [33093433428](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/actions/runs/33093433428) | 0s, nothing to restore | 3h31m33s |

A save at 2026-08-26T21:12Z was gone by the next build at 2026-08-27T16:29Z, which then paid a full cold compile. A save at 2026-08-27T20:04Z is still present a day later. Both entries are the same size, so exceeding the cap does not by itself explain which one survives.

The cached directory holds more than compile output. `external/` and `cache/repos/` carry fetched repositories including the CUDA 13 redistributables, which cost minutes to download again, while `execroot/.../bazel-out` carries the object files that cost hours to rebuild. No size breakdown has been taken, so which part dominates the 11.6 GB is unknown, and that is the first thing needed.

Impact is bounded. Builds run only on pushes to `main` that touch the wheel, so this costs 3½ hours on a refresh or a build-script change, not on routine work. Promotion runs from a published candidate and never compiles.

Done when:

- a size breakdown of the bazel output base is recorded from a build that runs anyway
- the cached content is small enough to be retained between consecutive builds
- two consecutive builds restore the cache, and the second compiles in minutes rather than hours

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
On 64 H100 (CoreWeave cw-us-east-02a, JAX 0.11.1, Snowball e12 FP32 SFT, 8x8 mesh, `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`), the same `jit_train_step` executable runs at about 122 s/step in the process that compiled it, and at about 45 s/step in a fresh process that loads it from the persistent JAX compilation cache. The cause is not known.

**Evidence**

| Run | Cache | Steady step |
|---|---|---:|
| Controlled pre-job (3 updates, empty cache) | miss, compile 14.2 s | 125.7, 122.5 s |
| Same config, next job, same cache URI | hit, 2.6 s | 49.4, 41.7, 44.4, 46.8 s |
| Distillation arm A, alpha 0 (compiled in-process; cache entry `jit_train_step-a19e8a54…`) | miss | 122 s (MFU 6.9%) |
| Same code and config, new job | hit on `a19e8a54…` (no new entry written) | 44.6, 41.2, 42.4, 47.4, 47.0, 38.1 s |

- The controlled test used one cache key, `jit_train_step-61378ece…`, in both stages. The executable fingerprint and compiled-text SHA256 match.
- The slow process is GPU-bound: ~350 of 411 s of a 3-step trace is on the compute stream, and ~100 s/step is in Triton GEMM fusions with small tiles (block 64, 768 B shared memory).
- Ruled out: autotune level (the fast program was also compiled at level 0, and the cached copy is the same executable), the per-fusion autotune cache (the cached autotune sets for the slow and fast trees match on 131,051 of 131,072 sampled keys), checkpointing, row content, and code version.
- Autotune level 4 was tried once: the compile finished in 41 s, but no step completed in 2.5 h (separate hang, not diagnosed).
- Compile records:
  - miss: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-fp32-redo-20261119/mochi-5cb/control-compile-prejob/compile-record.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-fp32-redo-20261119%2Fmochi-5cb%2Fcontrol-compile-prejob%2Fcompile-record.json))
  - hit: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-fp32-redo-20261119/mochi-5cb/control/compile-record.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-fp32-redo-20261119%2Fmochi-5cb%2Fcontrol%2Fcompile-record.json))
- Profile trace of the slow process: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/xprof/task504-distill-b-soft-20261119-profile/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Fxprof%2Ftask504-distill-b-soft-20261119-profile%2F))

**Why it matters**

The first run of any new config (code change, new schedule, new data shapes) compiles its own step and runs ~3x slower for its whole length. A config that differs from a warmed template looks 3x slower without anyone noticing why.

**Workaround**

Run a short warm-up job first: the same config, stopped after 3 updates, on the same `JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR`. Then start the real run and check that no new `jit_train_step` entry is written, or look for `Persistent compilation cache hit for 'jit_train_step'`.

**Open question**

What differs between the compiling process and a loading process? Candidates include a kernel choice made at compile time and then replaced on load, memory placement or allocator state left by compilation, and leftover autotuning buffers. A profile of both processes on the same executable would show which kernels differ.

Found by duiker (controlled test) and otter (task 504). Related: PR 11732.

**Relevant code**

1. On the same 8×8 H100 geometry, run a short cache-miss job followed by a cache-hit job with pinned source, image, `XLA_FLAGS`, input shapes, and cache URI. Record at least three unprofiled steady steps in each. Verify the cache key, executable fingerprint, and optimized HLO match before interpreting timing.
2. Capture two or three steady XPlane steps from each process at the same relative update. Compare kernel names, launch counts, GEMM tile choices, per-kernel duration, compute/collective time, and idle gaps with `profile_summary.py`. Confirm profiling preserves the slow/fast ordering; the existing slow-only trace cannot make this comparison.
3. If kernel choices differ, inspect XLA compile/load and autotune decisions. If choices match but runtimes differ, compare `cuda_async` allocator state, scratch availability, module-load activity, and direct compiled-executable versus stock JIT dispatch. Keep the executable and workload fixed while changing one runtime condition at a time.
4. Patch the isolated cause in Marin or report a minimal JAX/XLA replay upstream. Qualify a fix with repeated short miss/hit pairs, finite losses, no new cache entry on hits, and a steady-step gap below 10%.

| Run (64 H100, cw-us-east-02a) | Rank 0 rebind | Outcome |

If process 0 is still rebinding after `--xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds` (600 s in the e12 runtime profile), they fail with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED: GetKeyValue() timed out with key: cuda:root_process: 0`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Extended in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11909 with a 33-run 64-H100 audit (including the per-GPU power asymmetry, the `cw-rno2a` third mode, and a source check of Iris's one-fetcher-per-node autotune role).
A per-rank executable-fingerprint test after an in-job compile is queued there to check whether ranks 1–7 diverge from process 0.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Root cause (from runs already reported in issues 11793, 11909 and 11935): the ranks of an in-job compile do not run the same executable.**

The claim in this issue's first line, that "the same executable" runs in both processes, was checked on rank 0 only. That claim is wrong for the other ranks.

**How it happens**
- In an in-job compile, each of the 64 processes compiles its own executable. XLA reads that process's own per-fusion autotune folder, even at `--xla_gpu_autotune_level=0`.
- On `main`, only process 0 (uploader) and the first process on each other node (fetcher) fetch the tuned set (`compile_cache.py`, `_autotune_cache_role`). The other 56 processes compile from sparse or stale folders. They get untuned kernels: small-tile Triton GEMMs in place of cuBLASLt.
- The step is synchronous across ranks, so it runs at the speed of the untuned ranks, about 122–129 s.
- Only process 0 writes the persistent cache entry, and its executable is the tuned one. A later job loads that entry on all 64 ranks, so every rank runs tuned kernels, at about 45 s.

**Evidence**

| Test (64 H100, cold compile unless noted) | Distinct executables | Steady step |
|---|---:|---:|
| Default per-process folders (control, issue 11793) | 24 (another run: 3, as 56 + 7 + 1) | hung at step 0 |
| One empty folder on all ranks (issue 11793, two regions) | 1 | 121–130 s |
| One tuned folder on all ranks, read mode, 246,247 files (issue 11793) | 1 | 47.9–48.9 s |
| Cache hit on process 0's tuned entry (this issue) | 1, loaded | 42–49 s |

- **Not compile vs. load:** a cold compile from uniform tuned inputs runs at the fast rate. Compiling in the process does not by itself slow the step; the untuned kernels do.
- **The slow trace here was an untuned rank:** this issue's profile came from process 3 on rank 0's node, a rank that fetches nothing (see issue 11909).
- **Power fits the split:** in slow runs, the first GPU on each node (the rank that fetches the tuned set) draws about half the power of the others, on 8 of 8 nodes. It waits for the untuned ranks.

**Not shown**
- Per-rank executable hashes for this issue's own miss/hit pair were never recorded; the per-rank split above comes from matched runs of the same config in issue 11793.
- The tuned-folder run is n = 1, on a different node set and at a different time from its control.

**Fix status**
- PR 12423 makes every rank compile from one pinned, read-only snapshot.
- Without a configured `IRIS_AUTOTUNE_STORE_ROOT`, that snapshot is `empty`, and every new multi-GPU compile gets the untuned rate. The warm-up workaround above then stops helping too, since process 0's cached executable is also untuned. Details are in my review on PR 12423.
- The fix for this issue is PR 12423 together with a seeded, tuned regional snapshot. Next I will check that on a cold compile.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **How PR 11923 and PR 12423 fit together, and what should block the merge.**

- **PR 11923, the post-compile guard, turns the silent slowdown into a hard failure.** It compares each rank's optimized-HLO hash after compile and fails before step 0 if any rank differs. The slow in-job compiles reported here have ranks with tuned and untuned executables (see issue 11793), so the guard would stop them at start-up.
- **Merge order matters.** If PR 11923 lands without PR 12423, every in-job multi-GPU compile with today's per-process autotune folders should fail at start-up. A compile pre-job would not help, because the pre-job compiles in-job too. Only a run that hits an existing cache entry would start. Landing the two together, or PR 12423 first, avoids that.
- **What should block PR 12423's merge.** Without `IRIS_AUTOTUNE_STORE_ROOT`, every rank gets the `empty` snapshot. That fixes the mismatch, but at the untuned rate, about 125 s against 45 s per step on the 64-H100 e12 step. It also stops the pre-job workaround from working. PR 12423 should ship with either:
  1. a seeded, regional, compatibility-keyed tuned snapshot used by default for H100 jobs, or
  2. a fallback that gives every rank the same fetched tuned set (one fetch, shared read-only), not `empty`.
- **Validation status:** pinned-snapshot staging works across 36 of 36 logged ranks (see PR 12423). The cold-compile step time with a seeded snapshot is still not measured, because the e12 template's inputs are gone.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Validation of PR 12423 with a seeded tuned snapshot: the train step works, but an eval program failed.

Setup:
- Job `/karan/task504-distill-1h-a-hard-20261128c-i11775v3`: 64 H100 in 02a.
- Code: PR 12423 plus the PR 11923 compile guard.
- Compile cache: a new empty JAX cache, so every rank compiles cold.
- Autotune: snapshot `58c1a2829ad24d0b96065cf55f1391ea` (246,247 tuned files).
- Start point: the e12 base checkpoints have expired, so the run resumes a kept checkpoint of the same model and optimizer and runs 14 steps.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Snapshot staged | 64 of 64 ranks, same snapshot id, `file_count=246247` |
| Train step compile | Every train-step compile passed the cross-rank executable check, so all 64 ranks ran one executable |
| Steady train step, rank 0, steps 481–493 | 36.9–53.1 s, median about 47 s. The untuned path is about 125 s. |
| End-of-run eval (`jit_accum_for_batch`) | **Failed the guard: 13 distinct optimized-HLO hashes across 64 ranks** |

So with tuned data present, the cold-compiled train step matches the cache-hit speed. This supports the root cause posted earlier.

The eval failure is a separate open question:
- The pre-compile fingerprint check passed, so every rank gave XLA the same module.
- Every rank also read the same snapshot. Ranks on the same node, which share one staged folder, still produced different executables. For example, node 0's ranks fall into 5 hash groups.
- So uniform autotune files are not enough to make this compile deterministic.

I don't know the cause yet. My guess is that the eval fusions are not in this train-derived snapshot, and that a miss is not handled the same way on every rank, but I have not checked this. I've started a 1-step rerun with a fresh cache (`...20261128d-i11775v4`). It saves one optimized HLO per variant to S3, so the variants can be diffed directly.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on the eval mismatch: the cause is not autotuning.

The 1-step rerun with a fresh compile cache (`/karan/task504-distill-1h-a-hard-20261128d-i11775v4`) failed the same way on `jit_accum_for_batch`, this time with **17** distinct optimized-HLO hashes across 64 ranks. Some hashes are the same as in the 14-step run. I saved one optimized HLO per variant and compared them.

What the 17 variants show:
- **The Triton fusion configs are identical.** All 17 variants have the same 16 Triton fusions with the same block-level tile configs (ignoring stream-queue ids). So my guess that eval fusions miss the snapshot was wrong for this mismatch.
- **They diverge before scheduling.** Each variant carries a different `fingerprint_before_lhs`, so the modules already differ before the latency-hiding scheduler runs.
- **The difference is fusion structure.** It sits in small `s32[4,…]` slice/min/pad/concatenate trees in the model's mask/segment path (`jit(accum_for_batch)/Transformer/...`). Variants fuse different levels of a pairwise-min tree into a neighbouring fusion, and they have 148, 150 or 152 fusions.
- **The input was the same.** The pre-compile fingerprint matched on all ranks, and all ranks read the same autotune snapshot.

So XLA produced different fusion decisions for identical input on different processes. I don't yet know whether this is in-process nondeterminism or some per-process state. A third run (`...20261128e-i11775v5`) recompiles the same module 3 times inside each process after the mismatch and logs whether the hash is stable. If the hash varies inside one process, I'll file an upstream XLA issue with the module.

None of this changes the train-step result above: one executable on all ranks, about 47 s per step.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 The eval-program mismatch is nondeterministic compilation inside one process.

In the third run (`/karan/task504-distill-1h-a-hard-20261128e-i11775v5`), each process recompiled `jit_accum_for_batch` 3 more times right after the mismatch. It used `backend_compile_and_load` directly, so the persistent cache was not involved. Each process used the same `ir.Module`, devices and compile options as its first compile.

| Processes | Distinct optimized-HLO hashes over 4 compiles in one process |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 (stable) |
| 10 | 2 |
| 30 | 3 |
| 23 | 4 |

- 63 of 64 processes produced more than one optimized HLO for the same input.
- There were 31 distinct hashes across the job.
- The hash sets overlap between processes, so the variants are a pool of fusion outcomes, not per-rank states.

So this is not Marin or Iris state, and not the autotune cache. XLA's GPU compile of this module is nondeterministic. The earlier diff places the divergence in fusion decisions for small `s32` slice/min/pad/concatenate trees, before latency-hiding scheduling.

Next: a run (`...20261128f-i11775v6`) has process 0 compile the module twice with per-pass HLO dumps. The first pass whose outputs differ will go into an upstream XLA issue, with the dumped input module as the reproducer.

For PR 12423 and PR 11923 in the meantime:
- In-job cold compiles of this eval program will fail the executable check whatever autotune data is present.
- A persistent-cache hit avoids the problem, because every rank loads process 0's executable.
- The train step's cold compile was stable across all 64 ranks in both runs. I have not tested whether its compile is stable within one process.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 The eval-program nondeterminism is a known XLA bug. It is fixed upstream, but not in our jaxlib.

**Where it starts.** In `/karan/task504-distill-1h-a-hard-20261128f-i11775v6`, process 0 compiled `jit_accum_for_batch` twice with `xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.*`. The two compiles gave different results (`82588242…` and `9763270a…`), and each wrote 201 dump files.
- The last dump before fusion, `0126 fusion.after_pipeline-start`, is byte-identical between the two compiles. The passes between it and priority fusion did not change the module.
- The first output that differs is **`0127 fusion.after_priority-fusion`**. That diff has 3,374 changed lines, all in `jit(accum_for_batch)/Transformer` slice/min/pad/concatenate/add ops.

**Upstream.** This matches openxla/xla issue 49047, "GPU compilation is not reproducible: GpuHloCostAnalysis sums float utilizations in pointer-hash order, PriorityFusion near-ties flip between processes":
- `GpuHloCostAnalysis` sums per-root utilizations over a pointer-keyed `flat_hash_set`, so the float rounding depends on heap layout.
- Near-tied fusion priorities then flip.

That fits what we see. Each compile allocates at different addresses, so even recompiles inside one process differ.

**Versions.**

| Package | XLA commit | Contains the fix |
|---|---|---|
| jaxlib 0.11.1 (Marin's CUDA pin) | `dcf304bc5d` (2026-08-17) | no, 966 commits before it |
| jax 0.12.0 | `d867969800` | yes |
| jax 0.12.1 | `97b8433b3e` | yes |

The fix is openxla/xla commit `ee21092a8a`, "Use deterministic ordering for elementwise_use_roots_ in GpuHloCostAnalysis" (2026-09-22). No new upstream issue is needed.

**What this means here.**
- The same bug can in principle hit the train step too. It compiled to one executable on all 64 ranks in both runs, but that may be because this module has no near-ties at its fusion decisions. It is not a guarantee.
- With the PR 11923 guard, any in-job cold compile that hits a near-tie fails at start-up instead of running mixed executables.
- The real fix is moving the CUDA path to jax 0.12.x, or carrying a backport of `ee21092a8a`. I have not tested a jax 0.12 GPU run.

**Summary for issue 11775.**
1. The original 3× slowdown: per-rank autotune folders, where only process 0 and the per-node fetchers had tuned data. PR 12423 with a seeded snapshot fixes this; measured steady step about 47 s on a cold compile.
2. Cross-rank executable mismatches that remain after that: the upstream PriorityFusion nondeterminism above, fixed in jax 0.12.x.

spillover_issues.title: [levanter] GPU train step runs ~3x slower in the process that compiled it than when loaded from the persistent compile cache

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
We believe that formal verification is essential for open source models to get better at math, and better generally! Lean, a popular formal verification language primarily used for mathematical proofs, is one of the most popular avenues for this kind of improvement. We don't have RL data we trust for Lean, nor do we have evals we trust. Marin needs both in order to continue improving in this domain.

cc @Robertboy18

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin already grades Nemotron RLVR1 Lean responses with a pinned Lean 4.12/Mathlib compiler ([#10080](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10080), [#10088](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10088)). That establishes a reward path for those rows, but not an audited training corpus or held-out theorem-proving eval. [#10214](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214) excluded Lean from its mixed RLVR runs because Iris task pods could not start the Docker task machine; the [current eval policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) lists no Lean proof benchmark.

**Relevant code**
- [lean_grade.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemotron_ultra/lean_grade.py) — current compiler-backed reward.
- [lean.Dockerfile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemotron_ultra/lean.Dockerfile) — pinned toolchain and Mathlib.
- [lean_compiler.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-gym/skyrl_gym/lean_compiler.py) — task-local execution path.
- [proofpile.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datasets/proofpile.py) — existing pretraining corpus to check for overlap.

# Proposed Fix

1. **Freeze the eval first.** Inventory candidate Lean problem sets and record licenses, source revisions, theorem IDs, proof provenance, and required toolchains. Create public development and sealed test manifests; check statement/proof overlap against RLVR1, Proof-Pile 2, and proposed training sources. Specify prompts, token and time budgets, pass@1/pass@k, and how compiler failures and missing scores enter the denominator. Done when pinned reruns reproduce the same task IDs and verdicts.
2. **Audit the verifier.** Reuse the compiler path with controls for invalid proofs, `sorry`/`admit`, changed statements, extra axioms, and timeouts. Review a stratified sample of accepted and rejected attempts independently, publish disagreement counts, and resolve reward exploits before training. Keep the compiler and Mathlib revision identical between data validation and eval.
3. **Curate RL tasks.** Normalize licensed Lean statements and headers into provenance-bearing task records, deduplicate by theorem and near-duplicate text, and compile reference proofs where provided. Keep eval problems and their proof variants out of training. Resolve the Iris task-pod execution gap seen in #10214, then run a real task-session smoke test. Done when each released row has a source, toolchain pin, verification outcome, and contamination decision.
4. **Measure transfer.** Run pinned baseline models on the frozen eval, reporting pass@1/pass@k with uncertainty, per-source scores, and compiler/error rates. Compare a small Lean RL pilot against its starting checkpoint on the same eval and publish the dataset and run revisions. Expand the data or training budget only if the audited reward and held-out scores support it.

comments.author: Robertboy18
comments.body:
Thanks! I looked through what's out there, and a few things seem worth starting from:

- **One Lean version for data and evals.** I'd suggest v4.34.1: it has the fix for a kernel bug that allowed an axiom-free proof of `False` (leanprover/lean4#14576), and it's what Prime Intellect's Lean environments and openai/math use.
- **Evals:** [PutnamBench](https://github.com/trishullab/PutnamBench), [miniF2F (DeepMind fork)](https://github.com/google-deepmind/miniF2F) and [ProofNet-Verified](https://github.com/marcusm117/ProofNet-Verified), with [Lean Eval](https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval) as a hard ceiling.
- **RL data:** [Goedel RL_dataset_V2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Goedel-LM/RL_dataset_V2), [NuminaMath-LEAN](https://huggingface.co/datasets/project-numina/NuminaMath-LEAN) and [Kimina](https://huggingface.co/datasets/project-numina/Kimina-Prover-Promptset), plus [mathlib-tactics](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mathlib-initiative/mathlib-tactics) for SFT warm-up.
- **Environments:** [Prime's Lean environments](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-envs/tree/main/environments/lean) have the strictest grader I found and already filter these datasets for v4.34. Their env code only runs on Prime's VMs, but the image and checker are Apache-2.0, so we could reuse them in Harbor. [FineEnvs/openai-math](https://huggingface.co/datasets/FineEnvs/openai-math) runs on Harbor today.

One gap: nobody has the code-verification benchmarks (VERINA, CLEVER, Vericoding, FVSpec) on one version yet. I have them internally and will make them public once I've upgraded them all to v4.34.1. Which track would you like first?

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 A reward-floor check on the NuminaMath-LEAN training tasks from #11095, before the first Lean RL run. I rebuilt the 4,035 tasks with the recipe's own `row_contract` on main `2bf3f721c`, drew 1,000 at random and compiled fixed replies against each statement in the grader's proof-term form, with the grader image's Lean v4.34.1 and Mathlib `d13f23b`. 795 of the 1,000 were graded in the time I had (the first 300 in order, then a random part of the other 700); the shares weight the two parts by their size.

| Fixed reply | Tasks proved (95% interval) |
|---|---|
| `grind` | 19% (16.5-22%) |
| `first \| (rfl; done) \| (decide; done) \| ... \| (exact?; done)` over 15 tactics | 25% (22-28%) |
| any one of `simp`, `norm_num`, `decide`, `omega`, `linarith`, `exact?`, `aesop`, `trivial`, `rfl` | 17% (14-19%) |

So about 1,000 of the 4,035 tasks give reward 1 to one constant reply. On ProofNet-Verified, `simp`, `simp_all`, `aesop`, `grind`, `tauto`, `ring` and `exact?` proved 49 of 366 rows through the grader (13%, in my #10879 review); those seven prove 24% here. Every task has a compiling human proof, so none is false, but in a random 200, `grind` derives `False` from the hypotheses of 4.

I read 20 of the proved tasks. 16 are faithful but easy: final computations such as `algebra_15505` (`gcd 2835 8960 = 35`), and answers that follow from the stated equations. 4 state less than their problem:

- `algebra_13062` (`fbf349fa`): `h : ∀ x, x ≠ 3 ∧ x ≠ -5 ∧ ...` is false at `x = 3`.
- `algebra_160868` (`ec81e530`): `∀ n, F n = F (n - 1) + F (n - 2)` over ℕ forces `F 0 = 0`, but `F 0 = 1`.
- `algebra_235251` (`f7637b05`): the equation that solves the frog problem is a hypothesis.
- `Number_Theory_640629` (`ed0dad30`): the egg problem became a statement whose inner condition cannot hold, so it is true for every `m`.

Two more have contradictory hypotheses: `algebra_174839` (`c1528388`) and `combinatorics_609372` (`3962696e`, `r = 50`, `b = 50`, `r - b = 5`).

A group in which every sample succeeds has no advantage, so most of these tasks only cost rollouts, and the vacuous ones reward a reply that ignores the problem. Grading the `first | ...` reply once per task at curation takes about 4 s a task in a batch. Would a filter, or a difficulty tag for the curriculum, be useful? I can add either to the recipe.

comments.author: Robertboy18
comments.body:
Thanks Xiaoyuan, this is really useful! Yes please, I think both would help:
- Drop the tasks whose hypotheses already prove `False` (your `grind` check), since any reply gets reward there.
- Tag the rest by whether the fixed `first | ...` reply proves them, so the selection recipe can drop or downweight the easy ones. Small models may still learn from them, so a tag seems better than a hard filter.

The ones that state less than the problem, like `algebra_235251` and `Number_Theory_640629`, won't show up in either check. On #11526 we ran the human problem text through a judge against the Lean for every row, and it caught a lot of these, so I'm happy to run the same thing over the 4,035 and send you the list :)

Your judge list would be great, since neither check sees the statements that say less than their problem; I'm happy to fold it in once you have it.

comments.author: BirgerMoell
comments.body:
Related to steps 2 and 3: we've built an open set of Lean tasks with a verifier built to resist reward exploits. It may be a useful input, especially for the verifier audit and the RL curation.

Lean Arena (Renaissance Labs): https://huggingface.co/datasets/RenaissanceLabsEU/math, with a map of the 63 MSC areas and their Mathlib coverage at https://math.renaissancelabs.eu/

Tasks: 972 tasks in 9 environments (inequalities, group theory, linear algebra, real analysis, finite sums, and more). Each environment has 84 train and 24 eval tasks at three difficulty levels. A model fills in Solution.lean, or writes a definition. The tasks are in Harbor format.
Generated, not scraped: every task comes from a seeded generator, so each row has a seed, a family and a difficulty, and the dataset can't overlap with miniF2F, PutnamBench or Proof-Pile. Fresh seeds give unlimited new tasks.
Verifier: Verify.lean loads the hidden reference and the submission and compares kernel terms. It requires that the task's own definitions are unchanged, that the statement matches exactly, and that the proof uses only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. We also re-check with leanchecker. sorry, native_decide, a user axiom, a changed definition and a weakened statement are all rejected, and tools/verifier_cheats.py tests each of these.
Container check: we ran it with no network on one held-out task per environment. The reference solution scored 1.0 and the untouched start file scored 0.0. Grading takes about 2.5 minutes per task, mostly importing Mathlib several times.

Caveats:

It's on Lean 4.29.1 with Mathlib 5e932f97, not v4.34.1. The generators don't depend on the version, but moving would mean regenerating and re-running the self-tests.
We have no model baseline yet. One automation tactic closes 15 of 192 sampled proving tasks, which is a floor for how much needs no real proof, not a model score.
The eval split is in distribution (same templates, different seeds). It's good for RL practice, but it's not a general theorem-proving benchmark and shouldn't replace miniF2F or PutnamBench.

We can discuss this more in the math channel.

spillover_issues.author: WhenWen
spillover_issues.body:
Opened on behalf of @WhenWen for the belay-wn research loop. Updates are posted here as results land.

**Question.** Why does MuonH (fixed-norm hyperball matrices) trail MuonW on KMA d768 fast_track? Can a weight-normalized optimizer beat a *fairly tuned* MuonW-family baseline? The work covers KMA d768 and the Belay ladder recipe (d512–d1280, plus the 8-minute d512 speedrun). All numbers are Paloma macro loss, and gaps under the 0.005 band count as ties.

**Current answer (2026-11-19).** With equal tuning, the weight-normalized forms tie tuned MuonC. Neither family leads anywhere.
- *Baseline.* The bar is MuonC (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285): MuonW with matrix decay λ·lr_t/lr_max and an AdamW head. Its decay is tuned per length: best λ is 0.2–0.4 on the speedrun, 0.2 at ladder d512, and about 0.1 at d768. Both families also use the same s(t)² head anneal and late matrix anneal ("tl-d schedule").
- *Speedrun, d512, 8 min.* nonsi (learned per-matrix radius on MuonH) + schedule, with its starting size tuned, against tuned MuonC + schedule: +0.0007 over nine held-out seeds (95% −0.0033 to +0.0046). Both beat the recipe's MuonH by about 0.011–0.016.
- *Ladder d512.* nonsi + schedule against MuonC (λ 0.2) + schedule: +0.0033 on fresh seeds 4–7, a tie.
- *Formula-cap ball.* A no-decay ball whose per-layer cap comes from a shape/LR law, with no retuning. It ties MuonC + schedule on all four rungs: −0.0031, −0.0011, +0.0048 and −0.0029, one seed each. It also ties on the speedrun (+0.0004 over six seeds).
- *Mechanism.* Loss is set first by rotation per step and second by how matrix size evolves, not by where size ends up. A fit on MuonC's settings alone predicts nonsi's loss from its rotation to within 0.002. The original MuonH–MuonW gap fits the same picture: MuonH's rotation and size were off the optimum.
- *Open: d1280.* softcap + schedule (tl-d) trails MuonC + schedule by 0.0158 on one seed. Running d1024 width on d1280's recipe does not reproduce this, and a second seed is running.

**Intake posts.** speedrun-track proposals for nonsi + schedule (#9514, comment 7019355085) and MuonC (λ 0.2) + schedule (#9514, comment 7019433555).

**Running now**
- An "unnormalized hyperball" baseline: MuonH's norm-relative step with no projection, plus MuonC- or MuonW-style decay. It is tuned like MuonC and becomes the bar wherever it wins.
- MuonC decay brackets at d768–d1280.
- nonsi + schedule at d768–d1280, with seed 2.
- A second d1280 seed for tl-d vs MuonC + schedule.

Runs log to W&B project `understanding-sam/research-loop-belay-wn`.

🤖 **Experiment log, part 1 of 3: the KMA d768 gap and the first weight-normalized fixes (2026-11-17)**

Setup: KMA d768 fast_track, batch 128, ctx 4096, 6,930 updates, 8×H100. Metric: final validation loss on the tuning split (plus a fixed held-out set once it was verified). Seeds are paired.

**Baselines reproduced**
- MuonW seeds 0/1/3: 2.51555 / 2.51564 / 2.5219 (four-seed mean 2.5182).
- MuonH seeds 0/1/2: 2.52054 / 2.52530 / 2.52428.
- Mean paired gap +0.0057 (+0.0064 over three paired seeds). On the fixed held-out set it is +0.0054, lower bound > 0.
- MuonW LR ×0.71 / ×1.41 is worse than ×1.
- Checkpoint restore is bitwise exact on H100, and interrupted-vs-uninterrupted continuation matches.

**Where the gap is** (log reads and swap runs)
- MuonH's deficit is front-loaded: +1.8 nats in the first 100 steps, about 0 by step 5000, then a ~0.006 loss in the final anneal.
- Swaps put the whole gap in the hidden-matrix update:
  - MuonW matrices + MuonH head/Adam groups: 2.5164.
  - MuonH matrices + MuonW Adam groups: 2.5218.
  - Gates and fallbacks don't matter.
- Rotation vs size, finals:
  - ShadowH (MuonW's rotation on fixed spheres) ends at MuonH's level: best 2.5273, ×0.5 2.5360, ×2 2.5441.
  - MuonH's rotation with MuonW's size law ends at 2.5112 / 2.5138.
  - So the gap is weight scale, not rotation.
- MuonW for the first 1,000 steps, then MuonH holding those sizes: 2.5078. MuonH's problem is mainly its first ~1,000 steps at the small init size.

**Candidates (MuonH step + some way to set the matrix size)**
- *Fixed bigger spheres* at 0.66× the update size: 2.5178 (seed 0), equal to MuonW's mean.
- *C2* (radius follows MuonW's size law in closed form): 2.5112 / 2.5138 on seeds 0–1. On held-out it is −0.006 / −0.003 vs MuonW.
- *C3* (grow by that law for 1,000 steps, then hold) on seeds 1–5:
  - −0.0057 vs original MuonW.
  - −0.0024 vs tuned MuonW (not claimed).
- *Radial MuonH* (learned log-radius per slice, Adam on ⟨G, W⟩):
  - 2.5047 / 2.5082 on seeds 0–1, about 0.01 below MuonW.
  - But radii ran away up to ~4,600× on slices whose output feeds a norm. Their radial gradient is rounding noise, and Adam with ε≈0 turns it into full steps.
- *softcap* (outward radius steps scaled by 1 − (s/c)², c = 2, capped at 7.4×):
  - Kept all of radial's gain: seeds 0–1 mean 2.5060. Any cap from 2.5× to 15× gives the same result, and 1.5× loses it.
  - Against the original MuonW on seeds 2–7: −0.0091 (bound −0.0056), held-out −0.012.
- *nonsi* (no learned radius on the scale-invariant slices, no cap):
  - Seeds 0–1 mean 2.5064.
  - Learning radii for only the first 500 steps keeps almost all of the gain (2.5084).
- Closed negatives:
  - gradient-gated or slower learned sizes: ~2.517
  - coupled learned size: 2.544–2.552
  - adaptive step rules: 2.62–2.67
  - persistence: 2.520

🤖 **Experiment log, part 3 of 3: new weight-normalized forms, the mechanism, and what is running (2026-11-18 → 11-19)**

**Forms that did not beat MuonC (KMA d768, two seeds, same commit unless noted)**
- *Weight-normalized MuonC* (radius follows MuonC's decay law): 2.5121 / 2.5148, which is +0.011 vs MuonC. Changing decay moved the size 5× but the loss only ≤ 0.004.
- *ShadowC* (MuonC's rotation on a sphere): 2.5189 at init radius. With softcap's learned radius it gets 2.5086 (λ0.1), still worse than plain softcap.
- *Learned gain on MuonC* (MuonW family): adds nothing (+0.0007 to +0.0034). A weight-normalized head on MuonC's matrices costs about 0.
- *Four new constraint shapes, all with interior LR brackets:*
  - spectral-norm sphere: 2.4994, ties tl-d, −0.0018 behind MuonC + schedule
  - capped ball: +0.0020 vs tl-d
  - per-row radii: +0.0030 vs tl-d
  - Stiefel/orthogonal: about 0.10 worse; the constraint was verified exact, so this is real
- *Per-family caps* on the formula-cap ball: no gain (−0.0008 to +0.0092). *Caps at a fixed multiple of init:* best +0.003 vs the law cap.

**Forms that tie MuonC**
- *Formula-cap ball* (no decay; per-layer cap = 0.71·√(39·lr_max/(2·0.1))·|U_l|):
  - KMA d768: 2.4978 vs MuonC + schedule 2.4967.
  - Belay ladder vs same-commit MuonC (λ0.1) + schedule: −0.0031 / −0.0011 / +0.0048 / −0.0029 (d512–d1280).
  - Speedrun: +0.0004 over six seeds vs MuonC λ0.4.
  - It beats tl-d by 0.018 at d1280.
- *Ball capped at MuonC's measured final sizes* (explanation only): 2.49695 vs 2.49694.

**Mechanism, measured**
- Rotation per step is the first variable. Across MuonC and nonsi settings it explains loss with R² 0.97 on the ladder; final matrix size explains 0.02. A fit on MuonC's settings alone predicts nonsi's loss to within 0.002.
- Size is second, and it is the path over training that matters, not the end point:
  - Pinning nonsi at MuonC's final per-layer sizes loses ~0.009.
  - nonsi at start ×4 ends at MuonC's size with the same rotation and is 0.008 worse.
- In this recipe MuonC's matrices grow toward a fixed per-layer size and hold, without shrinking late.
- The formula-cap ball behaves like MuonC at about 1.2× its nominal decay, which is why its larger cap ties and its smaller cap loses.
- tl-d's d1280 loss is not radius stranding; tl-d's radii there are larger than softcap's. d1024 width on d1280's recipe does not reproduce it: nonsi + schedule and MuonC + schedule both score 2.3478 there.
- The original KMA H–W gap fits the same picture: MuonH's rotation and its size path were away from the optimum early on.

**Running now**
- *Unnormalized hyperball (uhs).* MuonH's step relative to the current norm (MuonH's tuned angular step, no projection), plus MuonC- or MuonW-style decay, with MuonC's AdamW head (0.35×, s² anneal in the schedule cells). Decay is bracketed per rung around its own balance point. Speedrun first, then the ladder. It replaces MuonC as a rung's bar if it wins.
- *MuonC decay brackets:* λ0.05 at d768; λ0.2 at d1024/d1280, run as H100 and GB200 sets.
- *nonsi + schedule:* d1024/d1280, seed 2, and d1280 head-only / anneal-only splits.
- *d1280 seed 2* for tl-d vs MuonC + schedule.
- *Formula-cap ball:* no-schedule pair at d1280.

All comparisons are now scored on the same hardware type. A difference between hardware types is only allowed as a difference of same-hardware differences.

🤖 **Update, 2026-11-19 23:25 → 11-20 00:45 PST**

**Goal change.** The target is now a weight-normalized optimizer that *beats* tuned MuonC + the s² anneals; a tie no longer counts. New lines should be designs derived from the measured mechanism, not new grids on existing forms (tuning only as much as a fair comparison needs).

- **d1280, seed 1 (lna):** nonsi + anneals trails same-code tuned MuonC by **+0.0086**, like tl-d. The cause is a smooth exponential drift of matrix size with no restoring force. The law-cap ball held at d1280 (−0.0029), so it is the only weight-normalized form that has kept pace on every rung. New designs will be confirmed on it.
- **Train-vs-Paloma offset (tdg, 308 speedrun runs, 260 pairs):** weight-normalized forms trail MuonC 0.005–0.008 more on training loss than on Paloma. This tracks the head's end size and logit scale (R² 0.75–0.80), not matrix size (0.15) or rotation (0.23), and is spread evenly over the 16 Paloma domains. It is a head trait, not a cost of weight normalization, and no held-out gain is hidden behind it.
- **Momentum echo (derivation, then a check):** each Muon update points back along its own recent steps through momentum, so ⟨Ô, Ŵ⟩ ≈ −κθ with κ ≈ 10.7. This accounts for the radial drift of the unnormalized hyperball and for the KDA w_beta runaway. It predicted the d512-ladder neutral decay at 0.152; the smoke run measured 0.166.
- **Direction noise (KMA d768):** about 80% of each Muon step goes along the momentum's noise-like directions, which hold only ~20% of its energy.

- A saturating law, c = 8 / (gain growth over the run), gives 2.18 / 1.66 / 1.55 / 1.55 / 1.60 from the speedrun to d1280. That is within 0.18 in log of every measured best ratio. It also predicts KMA d768's end gain (4.22 vs ~4.2 measured) with no new fit. It still has two constants taken from measurement.
- Next tests:
  - d768 held out (fitted law 1.44 vs saturating law 1.55 vs measured 1.36);
  - d512 at twice the steps, to tell whether the gain stops at a fixed point or because Adam's updates run out;
  - the learned temperature on fresh d512 seeds and at d1024/d1280;
  - a return to KMA d768 against a same-stack MuonC + anneals bar.

**Why the forms tie, and what is next.** The planner wrote out the premises behind the weight-normalized ≈ MuonC equivalence:
1. Muon's near-constant step size.
2. A Frobenius-norm constraint that decay relaxes.
3. Slowly varying per-slice rules that MuonC copies by scaling LR and decay together.
4. A fixed norm target.
5. A free weight spectrum.

Two new designs break premises no earlier line broke:
- **A Schatten-4 ball** caps runaway top singular values and leaves the rest of the spectrum and Muon's step alone. No scalar decay can express it. It is tested at the speedrun against tuned MuonC, the Frobenius law ball, and MuonC given matching Schatten-4 shrinkage.
- **One sphere coupling all residual-stream writers** fixes their total size and leaves the ratios free. It is tested at d1024, where weight-normalized trails MuonC by about 0.004, against MuonC with per-writer gains.

Per-row spheres were not run: row-normalized MuonC is their exact decay twin, so they can only tie. Earlier KMA runs already covered Stiefel (+0.106), the spectral sphere (+0.0018) and per-row radii (+0.0046).

🤖 **Update, 2026-11-24 09:15 → 11-27 15:30 PST**

**Direction.** The search now tunes one recipe family: softcap radial MuonH with the AIR angle schedule (Yu et al., arXiv 2610.40362), tuning the effective LR, AIR's alpha and cumulative angle, and the Adam LR. One seed per configuration; no new MuonC runs (the frozen MuonC bar is read from its finished runs). X0250 is the fixed external reference.

**Current best recipe** (softcap + AIR alpha/K 1/4, C 1.05 + s(t)² head + hlw + token_embed LR ×4), Paloma macro, against X0250's published numbers:

| Setting | ours | X0250 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| speedrun | 3.0222 (mean of 6 seeds, v4/v5e) | 3.0269 | −0.005 |
| d512 | 2.8427 (seed 446, H100) | 2.8503 | −0.008 |
| d768 | 2.5908 (seed 7, H100; uniform Adam ×4 in place of embed ×4) | 2.5990 | −0.008 |
| d1024 / d1280 | running | ~2.399 / ~2.260 | — |

X0250 is one seed per setting and speedrun seed noise is about 0.007, so the speedrun gap is not significant yet.

**What carries the gain** (same seed, one change at a time):
- AIR itself is worth about −0.004 at the bar's Adam LR at both the speedrun and d512. Without AIR, raising the Adam LR does not help.
- token_embed LR ×4 beats Adam ×1 by −0.0053 (6 seeds) and ties uniform Adam ×1.4.
- At d768, WN\* (nonsi + hlw + fh0.2 front-heavy schedule) beats the same-seed frozen MuonC by −0.0087 on 5 of 5 seeds; AIR (seed 7) by −0.0069.

**Closed or negative.**
- Adding tl-d's late tail on top of tuned AIR: +0.004.
- Replaying MuonC's measured anneal-phase angle path: +0.001 to +0.004 (4 pairs). The mid-run lead that the anneal removes is AIR's schedule phase, not headroom.
- The bar's AdamW fallback decay (hyb-an) at matched Adam LR, a row-sphere token embedding, and tighter radius caps: no gain.

**Finding.** Uncapped learned radius (nonsi) blows up on one slice, layer-0 KDA `w_k`: its norm grows from 38.7 to 1e7–6e8 in every d768 run, while every other slice stays within log-radius −2.4 to +1.0. Softcap (cap 2) holds the same slice at +0.78, so softcap is the radius control going forward.

**Infrastructure.** Speedruns can now run as one job on a whole v4-128 slice (64 chips): 0.44 s/step against 5.49 s/step on a 4-chip host, about 25–30 minutes per speedrun, with matching losses in a 40-step check.

**Running.** The recipe without hlw, with one-change ablations around it (carrier, Adam knob, fh0.2, alpha/K, C, decay-to-zero), on the speedrun; the same recipe at d512 and d768; the recipe with hlw at d1024 (seed 2) and d1280 (seeds 1 and 2). Two ladder proposals are posted on the Belay intake (#9514): WN\* and the AIR recipe.

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
14,062 of the 65,559 tasks of `NeMo:predicted-action` (21.4%) expect a string argument of 10 or more words that occurs nowhere in the request. The source scores a reply 1 only for the exact function name with exact JSON arguments ([`nemo_tool_calls.py` L37](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemo_tool_calls.py#L37), [`grade_predicted_action_candidate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_predicted_action.py#L47-L61)), so a reply passes such a task only when it writes that string character for character. In 13,738 of the 14,062 tasks the only such arguments are `summary` or `issue_summary`, with a median of 32 words. They belong to calls that hand the conversation to a person, such as `transfer_to_human_agent`.

EvalLite's `agents` family is 165 tasks of this source ([recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/experiments/post_training/task_curation/recipes/eval-lite.json#L78-L86)). At the source's rate about 35 of them are such tasks, and every checkpoint scores 0 on them. The recipe's seeded order selects 44 when I apply it to the source without the overlap exclusions; I cannot read the training and development sets that the exclusions use.

Reproduce:

1. One task, row 94,789 of the pinned `train.jsonl`. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   uv run --package marin-verifyit python - <<'EOF'
   from verifyit.modes.grade_predicted_action import grade_predicted_action_candidate
   from verifyit.spec import FunctionCall, PredictedActionSpec

   expected = (
       "User inherited portfolio with appreciated securities, questions about step-up basis calculation "
       "and tax implications of significant gains."
   )
   spec = PredictedActionSpec(
       expected_calls=(FunctionCall("transfer_to_human_advisor", {"summary": expected, "urgency": "medium"}),)
   )
   replies = (
       expected,
       expected.rstrip("."),
       "The user inherited a portfolio of appreciated securities and asks how the step-up in basis is "
       "calculated and what tax the gains carry.",
   )
   for reply in replies:
       call = FunctionCall("transfer_to_human_advisor", {"summary": reply, "urgency": "medium"})
       print(grade_predicted_action_candidate(spec, (call,)).reward, reply)
   EOF
   ```

   It prints `1.0` for the expected call, `0.0` for the same call without the final period of the summary, and `0.0` for a paraphrase of the summary.

2. The count. The command downloads the pinned `train.jsonl` (1.75 GB) and takes about two minutes:

   ```bash
   uv run --package marin-taskcompendium python - <<'EOF'
   import json
   import statistics

   from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
   from taskcompendium.identity import canonical_sha256
   from taskcompendium.importers.nemo_predicted_action import DATASET, REVISION, import_row


   def texts(value):
       """Every string in a JSON value, and every string inside a string that is itself JSON."""
       if isinstance(value, str):
           yield value
           try:
               value = json.loads(value)
           except ValueError:
               return
           if not isinstance(value, dict | list):
               return
       for item in value.values() if isinstance(value, dict) else value if isinstance(value, list) else ():
           yield from texts(item)


   tasks, free_rows, long_rows, summary_only, longest = 0, 0, 0, 0, []
   with open(hf_hub_download(DATASET, "train.jsonl", revision=REVISION, repo_type="dataset")) as rows:
       for line in rows:
           row = json.loads(line)
           try:
               task = import_row(row, canonical_sha256(row))
           except ValueError:
               continue
           tasks += 1
           seen = "\n".join(texts(row["responses_create_params"]))
           free = {
               key: len(value.split())
               for call in task.grader.parameters["expected_calls"]
               for key, value in call["arguments"].items()
               if isinstance(value, str) and len(value.split()) >= 2 and value not in seen
           }
           free_rows += bool(free)
           if free and max(free.values()) >= 10:
               long_rows += 1
               summary_only += {key for key, words in free.items() if words >= 10} <= {"summary", "issue_summary"}
               longest.append(max(free.values()))
   print(tasks, free_rows, long_rows, summary_only, statistics.median(longest))
   EOF
   ```

   It prints `65559 15164 14062 13738 32.0`: the tasks, the tasks that expect a string of two or more words that is absent from the request, the tasks where such a string has 10 or more words, the tasks among those where only `summary` or `issue_summary` holds such a string, and the median word count of the longest such string.

Expected: a task whose expected call holds free text is left out of the source, or its free-text arguments are compared by a rule that a correct reply can meet.

NeMo Gym's verifier for this dataset compares strings of two or more words by word overlap, with a threshold of 0.1 ([config L7-L8](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/69a514999667cebee03d8fd8bd0aec996a54a504/resources_servers/single_step_tool_use_with_argument_comparison/configs/single_step_tool_use_with_argument_comparison.yaml#L7-L8), [`_compare_strings`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/69a514999667cebee03d8fd8bd0aec996a54a504/resources_servers/single_step_tool_use_with_argument_comparison/common/verification_utils.py#L597-L634)). The paraphrase of step 1 has an overlap of 0.225 under that rule. The dataset stores 16 rewards per row for Qwen3-235B (`qwen_235b_info`). Their mean is 0.40 on the 14,062 rows and 0.33 on the 46,162 rows whose expected string arguments are all single tokens.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
On the Atlas branch (`atlas-env-audit`, open PR #11277), the LeetCodeDataset grader ships without the harness module it imports, so every non-empty reply is recorded as an infrastructure error and only empty replies, already 0, reach the loss. LeetCodeDataset was admitted 2026-11-27 (2,639 tasks).

[`leetcode_grade.py:19`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/leetcode_grade.py#L19) does `from leetcode_harness import harness_reward`, but the converter ships only the grade script: [`leetcode_dataset.py:36`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/leetcode_dataset.py#L36) reads `LCB_GRADE = grade_script(HERE / "leetcode_grade.py")`, so a converted task carries only `grade.py` and `config.json`. `test_leetcode_dataset.py:90` checks only the script text, so qualification never ran the grader.

Reproduce:
1. Check out `atlas-env-audit`, convert LeetCodeDataset, and open a converted task directory: it contains only `grade.py` and `config.json`.
2. Stage any non-empty reply at `/app/answer.txt` and run the shipped `grade.py`: it exits 1 with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'leetcode_harness'`.

Expected: the harness module ships with the grader script, and a non-empty reply grades through the source's own `check()` harness to 0 or 1; only harness defects exit nonzero as infrastructure errors.

Measured ([evidence comment on #11277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11277#issuecomment-7237269267)): on 60 seeded rows, the reference solution and 12 other non-empty replies all exit 1 with that `ModuleNotFoundError`.

Fix shape from the evidence comment: ship the harness next to the script, `grade_script(HERE / "leetcode_grade.py", *shipped_files(HERE, "leetcode_harness.py"))`, as [`skyrl/code.py:39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/code.py#L39) ships the APPS evaluator — and run `harness_reward` in a child process with the candidate's stdout kept out of the reward channel, as `skyrl/apps_grade.py` does: with the file present but in-process, a reply can print `1` and raise `SystemExit(0)` to score 1.0 (measured on all 60 references). The script's bytes are part of every TaskSpec, so the fix requires reconverting the source.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 I confirmed the Atlas converter packages `grade.py` and `config.json` without `leetcode_harness.py`. Running the staged script by itself exits with `ModuleNotFoundError` before it reads the reply. This affects the 2,639 tasks admitted for R41. [Converter](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/leetcode_dataset.py#L25-L36) · [Admission record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/373b500293d0c3748f8ab4ba861192e6919e4ded)

1. On `atlas-env-audit` (#11277), package `leetcode_harness.py` with `shipped_files`. Run the harness in a bounded child process with candidate output kept off reward stdout. The parent should emit the reward only from a validated harness result, score candidate failures and timeouts zero, and exit nonzero for harness defects. [APPS process pattern](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/apps_grade.py#L24-L54)
2. Add a regression that converts the existing LeetCode fixture, stages only the packaged resources, and runs the actual grader command. Assert that a correct reference emits 1, an incorrect reply emits 0 even if it writes output, and a broken harness exits nonzero. Check those outcomes in the pinned grader environment before publishing.
3. Bump the converter version and reconvert the 2,641 train rows from the existing upstream revision. Publish a new immutable retained release with a fresh census, deduplication, lexical measurement, and a SAMPLE panel for the new pin. Update the admitted-source registry binding and verify the Atlas consumer selects the new revision and grades the published TaskSpecs. [Admission binding](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/leetcode_dataset_admitted.py#L19-L33) · [Re-pin gates](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/docs/references/task-curation.md#L280-L287)

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
Under the shell harness, `grade_math` grades a plain-text final line that does not parse as a whole by one number taken from its text. A correct answer written as a sentence scores 0.0 for references such as `\sqrt{2}`, `\frac{\pi}{4}`, `(2,3)`, `\dfrac{1}{2}`, `\$5` and choice letters, and a wrong answer that starts with the reference's number scores 1.0.

The long-loop campaign runs its single-turn math tasks under the shell harness, which ends the prompt with the user turn "Give your answer as plain text." ([`submission.py` L210-L214](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ceb2e58074aeccfe2ab4f6ce89dfe73ca7e97a1/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/submission.py#L210-L214)). When the reply has no `\boxed{}`, `math_answer` grades its last line ([`grade_math.py` L605-L611](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ceb2e58074aeccfe2ab4f6ce89dfe73ca7e97a1/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L605-L611)). `_parse` ([L99-L114](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ceb2e58074aeccfe2ab4f6ce89dfe73ca7e97a1/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L99-L114)) wraps the line in `$...$`. When latex2sympy rejects the whole line, math-verify falls back to a number matched in the text, or to nothing when the line has none. #11973 describes that fallback for references, and #11989 fixed it for references only.

Reproduce, from the repository root:

```bash
uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra math python - <<'EOF'
from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_text_candidate
from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

CASES = (
    ("2", (r"The answer is 2.", r"The answer is 2\sqrt{3}.", "The answer is 2 or 3.")),
    ("-8", ("The answer is -8i.",)),
    (r"\frac{\pi}{4}", (r"\frac{\pi}{4}", r"The answer is \frac{\pi}{4}.", r"The answer is $\frac{\pi}{4}$.")),
    ("C", ("C", "C.", "The answer is C.", "Answer: C")),
)
for reference, replies in CASES:
    spec = MathSpec(expected=reference, math_type=MathType.SCALAR)
    print(reference, "|", ", ".join(f"{reply}: {grade_math_text_candidate(spec, reply).reward}" for reply in replies))
EOF
```

On main `3ceb2e58` it prints:

```
2 | The answer is 2.: 1.0, The answer is 2\sqrt{3}.: 1.0, The answer is 2 or 3.: 1.0
-8 | The answer is -8i.: 1.0
\frac{\pi}{4} | \frac{\pi}{4}: 1.0, The answer is \frac{\pi}{4}.: 0.0, The answer is $\frac{\pi}{4}$.: 1.0
C | C: 1.0, C.: 0.0, The answer is C.: 0.0, Answer: C: 0.0
```

I graded every row's own reference of the campaign's math sources through the long-loop runtime (`d5ca98a856`, the `pr/11120` head), as `\boxed{R}` and as `The answer is R.`:

| source | rows where `\boxed{R}` scores 1 | of them, `The answer is R.` scores 0 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `numina_math` (every row of NuminaMath-CoT, 859,494 before conversion) | 802,990 | 373,623 |
| `deepscaler` | 40,276 | 8,565 |
| `hardmath@rhs` | 684 | 554 |
| `hendrycks_math` (algebra) | 1,743 | 283 |
| `aime_1983_2024` | 933 | 1 |
| `dapo_math`, `gsm8k` | 17,405 and 7,473 | 0 and 0 |

The sentence still scores 1.0 on the other 429,319 `numina_math` rows, mostly plain numbers (314,726), `\frac` of two integers (43,569) and percentages (13,801).

106,592 of the `numina_math` rows have a choice letter alone as reference (`C`, `\text{B}`, `(C)`). On every one of them the letter scores 1.0, and `C.`, `The answer is C.` and `Answer: C` score 0.0.

The data also supplies wrong answers that pay. 11,426 `numina_math` rows have a plain-number reference and list answer choices. On 207 of them another choice starts with the reference's number and scores 1.0 as `The answer is <choice>.`, while the bare choice scores 0.0. Row 3141 of `train-00000-of-00005.parquet` has reference `-8` and choice C `-8i`; row 23396 has reference `2` and choice B `2\sqrt{3}` (rows count from 0).

`Answer: R` fares the same. `Answer: C` parses whole, as the ratio `Answer : C` (`(E*a*n*r*s*w)/c`), and the form scores 0.0 on 372,313 `numina_math` rows whose boxed answer pays. On 671 more, 608 of them equations, it exhausts the verifier deadline, so a correct reply becomes an infrastructure error; graded twice more, at least 632 of them exhausted it again both times.

`_parse` and `math_answer` are the same on main and at `d5ca98a856`. On a tenth of the `numina_math` specs, 64,977 of 65,059 rows get the same sentence outcome on both. I have not measured how often Mochi ends a math reply with a sentence, because the campaign's rollouts are not public.

Expected: the reward for a plain-text final line depends on the whole answer it states. `The answer is 2\sqrt{3}.` scores 0.0 against `2`, and `The answer is \frac{\pi}{4}.` scores 1.0 against `\frac{\pi}{4}`. spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
On the Atlas branch (`atlas-env-audit`, open PR #11277), `acecode_grade.py` runs the candidate's code outside any `try`, so a reply whose code fails to run is recorded as an infrastructure error instead of reward 0. The source notes promise "0 on any candidate-code failure; harness defects exit nonzero as infrastructure errors". Downstream, `_training_decision` (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py:185-208`) sets `loss_eligible=False` and `baseline_eligible=False` for a non-graded outcome, so the wrong reply takes no part in the loss or the baseline.

[`acecode_grade.py:21-22`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/acecode_grade.py#L21-L22) execs the reply's last fenced block unguarded. The script exits 1 when the reply does not compile, raises at module level, imports a package the grader image lacks, or is prose with no code; the most common case is `List[int]` in a signature without `from typing import List`, which raises `NameError` when the `def` runs, and a reply that never returns holds the script until the 330 s timeout. Each assert case below is already guarded ([L26-L30](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/88576a25205474c8475987bceb9beb33141c44e5/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/acecode_grade.py#L26-L30)); only the candidate's own exec is not. `test_acecode_89k.py:83` checks only that the script text contains `exec(case` and `print(1)`, so qualification never ran the grader.

Reproduce:
1. Check out `atlas-env-audit` and stage a converted AceCode task the way the converter's `_script_reward` does: `grade.py` at the task root, `config.json` at `/tests/`, reply at `/app/answer.txt`.
2. Write a reply whose last fenced block is

   ```python
   def f(xs: List[int]) -> int:
       return sum(xs)
   ```

   with no `from typing import List`.

3. Run the grader: `exec(code, namespace)` raises `NameError` outside any `try`, the script exits nonzero, and `_script_reward` records an infrastructure error.

Expected: a reply whose code fails to run scores 0; only harness defects exit nonzero as infrastructure errors.

Measured (full tables in the [evidence comment on #11277](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11277#issuecomment-7226075585)): grading the source's own sampled completions (up to 5 models x 16 per row) in a sandbox with no network and CPython 3.12 stdlib only, 3,828 of 24,016 completions (15.9%) on 306 rows, and 2,189 of 12,000 (18.2%) on 150 more, are infrastructure errors; 3,743 of the first sample's errors have source `pass_rate` 0. Causes in the first sample: `NameError` 1,832 (mostly unimported `List`/`Tuple`/`Union`), `SyntaxError` 1,049, `IndentationError` 585, `ModuleNotFoundError` 284, over a 10 s bound 20.

Fix shape from the evidence comment: run the candidate and its cases inside one `try` that also catches `SystemExit` and a `SIGALRM` budget, redirect the candidate's stdout, and print only 0 or 1; keep the nonempty-case-list assert outside. This also closes a smaller route of the class in #11990: the reward is the last stdout line, which the candidate shares, so a reply that prints `1` and then raises `SystemExit(0)` would score 1.

Two consequences to plan for, both from the evidence comment: tasks whose passing completions need a third-party package (at least 24 of 86,560, e.g. `yaml`) score 0 for every reply after the fix and need the package in the grader image or exclusion; and the script's bytes are part of every TaskSpec, so the fix requires reconverting the source's 86,560 tasks. The source routes to R41 intake (outside R40's frozen set), so this is still ahead of any run that uses the tasks.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
The Atlas ETL runs only on `atlas-env-audit` (draft #11277). This includes cross-source dedup, lexical decontamination, censuses, license receipts, fingerprints and SAMPLE QC. Main checks the hashes of the releases that branch published and cannot rerun any stage. The branch is about 2,250 commits ahead of main. In `experiments/post_training/task_curation` alone it adds about 132k lines, and none of the stage modules exist on main.

Following the direction in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12309#issuecomment-7209216514, the stages move into the existing taskcompendium `run_source_pipeline`. A FULL campaign on main then writes the retained population itself, and Hugging Face publication becomes a step that runs after it. Until cutover, releases still ship from the branch, and stage fixes there must also be ported to main.

Each stage PR is accepted when one source already declared on main reproduces its sealed branch release: retained task IDs and counts, stage marks and exclusions, and receipt digests match, or each difference has a reviewed explanation.

## Burndown

### 1. Read path
- [ ] #12362 lands (versioned `TaskStore` at the end of every campaign; its remaining review feedback is the author's).
- [ ] #12362's four incomplete sources and four unrun Lean sources are resolved or explicitly accounted for.
- [ ] #12309, #12321 and #12329 are closed. Keep any independent source declarations or checks that the reviewers name.

### 2. Stages in `lib/taskcompendium`
- [ ] Lexical measurement and decontamination. Reproduction source: ASDiv. Main's census yields 2,295 tasks against the sealed 2,305, because verifyit math grading now rejects 10 text answers; this needs a reviewed explanation or fix.
- [ ] Cross-source dedup
- [ ] Census (actor, grading and Daytona censuses)
- [ ] License receipt check (through the shared licensed-publish helper)
- [ ] Fingerprints and neighbor survey
- [ ] SAMPLE QC (panel freeze, review, receipt)
- [ ] Derived contracts and backend survey

### 3. Source families
Each family moves after its stages exist, as one or more PRs that reproduce its sealed releases.
- [ ] Math: Big-Math, Polaris, Reasoning Gym, HARDMath, Lean, Nemotron Ultra (incl. Lean and RDKit renames), Prime Intellect
- [ ] Code: AceCode-89K, LeetCode, LiteCoder, crosscode repair (C#, Java, TypeScript, Python), PyMethods2Test
- [ ] SWE and terminal: SWE-rebench V2.1, OpenSWE, SkyRL, MiMo, Terminal-Lego, TerminalWorld, CLI-Gym, Terminus, FACET terminal, native Harbor, Endless, Workplace
- [ ] Instruction following and formatting: IFBench, InverseIFEval, instruction hierarchy, Dolci precise-IF, StructEval, Nemotron structured outputs, TaskTrove structured native, citation, free-form and QA formatting
- [ ] Knowledge, QA and research: Nemotron MCQA, QA-Abstention, TaskTrove knowledge, Evalchemy, BrowseComp, Edge web search, OpenResearcher, S1 deep research, MCP-Atlas, PDBThink, Nemotron tool calls, RST, FineEnvs, structure closure, thoughtcrime
- [ ] Repair, oracle and backfill release families (repair, oracle, backfill and campaign releases, and the receipt directories)

### 4. Release
- [ ] Release graph as a taskcompendium publication step from a FULL main campaign
- [ ] RL data catalog UI: tracked separately in #12401; it lands after the ETL
- [ ] Harbor, shellbox, verifyit and rolloutengine changes the stages depend on, each upstreamed with its first consumer

### 5. Cutover
- [ ] One Atlas release built entirely from main, with receipts matching the branch release
- [ ] `atlas-env-audit` frozen. #11277 closes only after the catalog UI port in #12401, which lands after this issue.

Done when: an Atlas release is produced from main by a taskcompendium campaign, and `atlas-env-audit` no longer carries ETL code.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 The #12402 body's explanation holds for nine of the ten: they are text answers that main's math grader cannot grade. The tenth is a number that the converter destroys. I ran `ASDiv:asdiv` through `run_source_pipeline` at `04ba26139a` (2,305 rows in, 2,295 tasks) and graded every reference in process.

| ASDiv ID | answer field | rejected since |
|---|---|---|
| nluds-0030 | `Mrs. Hilt` | #11517 |
| nluds-1046 | `The men's track team` | #11517 |
| nluds-1051 | `Mrs. Doyle's class` | #11517 |
| nluds-1331 | `-(1/3)`, stored as `-` | #11517 |
| nluds-0868 | `The 60th caller.` | #11989 |
| nluds-0166 | `3:30 p.m.` | #11989 |
| nluds-1110 | `11:45 p.m.` | #11989 |
| nluds-2060 | `9:03:36 a.m.` | #11989 |
| nluds-2068 | `6:01:00 p.m.` | #11989 |
| nluds-1111 | `11:55 p.m. on 24 December 2014.` | #11989 |

With the conversion check bypassed, every reply to the nine raises `InvalidTask` at grade time. Normalizing fails: without `p.m.`, `3:30` reads as 1/10, so `\boxed{\frac{1}{10}}` scores 1 and `3:30 p.m.` scores 0. Without the period, `Mrs Hilt` is a product of letters, so `\boxed{tliH srM}` scores 1 and `Mrs. Hilt` scores 0; inside `\text{}`, only the exact string scores 1.

nluds-1331 asks for n in 5n + 7 = 2n + 6, and `ASDIV_UNITS` removes `(1/3)` as a unit. The same pattern removes only the last unit of 75 kept several-part answers, so `17 (years old); 12 (years old)` is stored as `17 (years old); 12`. On 52 of them, `\boxed{17, 12}`, `17 and 12`, `17 years old and 12 years old` and the answer field itself all score 0.

Removing every parenthesized group that contains a letter changes these 76 references and no others. nluds-1331 becomes `-(1/3)`: `\boxed{-\frac{1}{3}}`, `-1/3` and `The answer is -1/3.` score 1 and `\boxed{\frac{1}{3}}` scores 0. On the 75, the values score 1 and a wrong last value scores 0; order is not checked, and values written with units stop scoring on 23.

So the count is 2,295 with this list, or 2,296 with the pattern change. As [noted on #12402](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12402#issuecomment-7231707407), these tasks are lm-eval `asdiv` items, so the count only gates the stage's acceptance.
